name: Trinity nuclear test
summary: The first detonation of a nuclear weapon, in the New Mexico desert before dawn on 16 July 1945.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The Trinity test was the first detonation of a nuclear weapon. It was carried out by the Manhattan Project at 05:29 on 16 July 1945 on the Alamogordo Bombing Range in the New Mexico desert, about 340 kilometres south of the Los Alamos laboratory. The device, a plutonium implosion bomb the team called the Gadget, released energy equivalent to roughly 20 kilotonnes of TNT.

The test was held because the implosion design was uncertain. The gun-type uranium bomb later dropped on Hiroshima was thought reliable enough to use untried; the plutonium weapon, which was the one the project could build in quantity, was not. Observers watched from bunkers about nine kilometres away. The flash was seen hundreds of kilometres off, and the army told local newspapers that an ammunition magazine had exploded.

Weapons of the same programme were used on [Hiroshima and Nagasaki](event:hiroshima) three weeks later. Trinity is usually taken as the opening of the nuclear age; the desert sand fused by the blast into a pale green glass, named trinitite, is still there, and the site is a national historic landmark.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_(nuclear_test)).

name: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: The United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; Japan surrendered days later. They remain the only use of nuclear weapons in war.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). The United States detonated an atomic bomb over Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and a second over Nagasaki on 9 August. Estimates of the dead by the end of that year range from about 110,000 to 210,000, the great majority of them civilians. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. These remain the only uses of nuclear weapons in war.

The Hiroshima bomb, Little Boy, was a gun-type uranium weapon; the Nagasaki bomb, Fat Man, used the plutonium implosion design proved at [Trinity](event:trinity) three weeks earlier. Roughly half the deaths came on the first day, from blast and firestorm; the rest followed over weeks and months from burns, injuries and radiation sickness. Survivors, called hibakusha in Japan, faced long-term illness and social stigma.

The Soviet Union declared war on Japan and invaded Manchuria on 9 August, between the two bombings, and historians still argue over how much each pressure counted in Tokyo's decision to [surrender](event:vj-day). Nuclear arsenals were built up during the [Cold War](event:cold-war), and no nuclear weapon has been used in war since 1945.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bombings_of_Hiroshima_and_Nagasaki).

name: Victory in Europe
summary: Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945; the war in Europe ended on 8 May, and the continent was left divided where the armies had stopped.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945, ending the Second World War in Europe. The instrument of surrender was signed at Reims in the early hours of 7 May and ratified in Berlin late on 8 May. Britain, the United States and much of Western Europe mark 8 May as Victory in Europe Day; Russia and several of its neighbours mark 9 May, the date in Moscow time.

Hitler had killed himself in the Reich Chancellery bunker on 30 April as Soviet troops fought through the capital, and Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz headed the rump government that surrendered a week later. Unlike the armistice that ended [the First World War](event:ww1), the surrender left no room to argue that Germany had not been beaten in the field.

Victory in Europe was not peace. The continent was divided roughly where the armies had stopped; Germany and Berlin were split into four occupation zones; millions of displaced people and expelled German speakers were on the roads. The war against Japan ran on until [August](event:vj-day), and within two years the wartime alliance had become the [Cold War](event:cold-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_in_Europe_Day).

name: Victory over Japan
summary: Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945, ending the Second World War and beginning an American-led occupation that lasted until 1952.
body:
Part of [World War II](event:ww2). Japan's surrender ended the Second World War. Emperor Hirohito announced it by radio on 15 August 1945, and the formal instrument was signed aboard the battleship USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September. Britain and Japan mark 15 August; the United States marks 2 September.

The surrender followed the [atomic bombings](event:hiroshima) of Hiroshima and Nagasaki on 6 and 9 August and the Soviet declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria on 9 August. The Pacific war, which had begun for the United States with the attack on [Pearl Harbor](event:pearl-harbor), had lasted three years and eight months; across Asia and the Pacific it cost millions of lives, most of them Chinese and Japanese civilians.

The American-led occupation that followed wrote a new constitution renouncing war, broke up the industrial combines, redistributed farmland and tried the wartime leadership. Japan regained its sovereignty in 1952, though American bases remained and those on Okinawa are still contested. Korea was divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and American zones, a partition that led to the [Korean War](event:korean-war) five years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_over_Japan_Day).

name: United Nations founded
summary: Fifty nations signed the UN Charter at San Francisco in June 1945, creating a permanent international organisation with a Security Council that can authorise the use of force.
body:
The United Nations was created to keep the peace after the Second World War. Delegates from fifty countries met in San Francisco from April 1945 and signed the Charter on 26 June; it came into force on 24 October, now marked as United Nations Day. Poland signed shortly afterwards, making fifty-one original members.

The design tried to correct the weakness of the League of Nations by giving the organisation force to call on. The Security Council can impose sanctions and authorise military action, and its resolutions bind members. But its five permanent members (the United States, the Soviet Union and now Russia, China, Britain and France) each hold a veto, which left the Council deadlocked through most of the [Cold War](event:cold-war).

The General Assembly, where every member has one vote, grew from 51 states to 193 as [decolonisation](event:decolonisation) proceeded. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948. Much of the organisation's most visible work is done by its specialised agencies and programmes (the World Health Organization, UNICEF and UNHCR) and by peacekeeping forces deployed with the consent of the parties.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations).

name: Decolonisation
summary: Within thirty years of the Second World War the European overseas empires came apart, and some seventy new states took their place.
body:
Between 1945 and 1975 the European overseas empires dissolved. Britain, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Portugal withdrew from, or were driven out of, most of Asia and Africa. Membership of the [United Nations](event:un-founded) rose from 51 states to more than 140 over the same period, and the map of the world took roughly the shape it has now.

The war was the trigger. It had exhausted the imperial powers, destroyed the prestige of European rule in Asia, and armed and organised colonial populations. Both the United States and the Soviet Union were hostile to the old empires, for different reasons, and the [Cold War](event:cold-war) gave nationalist movements outside sponsors and leverage.

How it happened varied enormously. Some transfers were negotiated within a few years: [India and Pakistan](event:indian-independence) in 1947, Ghana in 1957, and most of French West and Equatorial Africa in 1960. Others were long wars: Indochina to 1954, Algeria from 1954 to 1962, and the Portuguese territories until the regime in Lisbon itself fell in 1974.

The new states inherited borders drawn by colonial administrators, economies built to export a few raw materials, and thin civil services. Several later conflicts (Kashmir after [partition](event:partition), Biafra, Congo and Rwanda) ran along lines the empires left behind.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonization).

steps.name: Independence in Asia (1945–1954)
steps.page: The first wave came in Asia, where Japanese conquest had broken European authority. The Philippines became independent of the United States in 1946. The Dutch fought a four-year war in Indonesia before recognising its independence in 1949. Burma and Ceylon left the British empire in 1948. France fought on in Indochina until the defeat at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954; Cambodia and Laos were already independent, and Vietnam was partitioned pending elections that were never held, the opening of [the Vietnam War](event:vietnam-war).

steps.name: The Algerian War (1954–1962)
steps.page: Algeria had been governed as part of France since 1848 and held about a million European settlers. The Front de Libération Nationale began an insurrection on 1 November 1954, and the war that followed involved half a million French troops, systematic torture, and the resettlement of much of the rural population. It brought down the Fourth Republic in 1958 and returned Charles de Gaulle to power. Independence came on 5 July 1962 after the Évian agreements; most of the settler population left within months. Estimates of the Algerian dead range from a quarter of a million to a million.

steps.name: Suez and the loss of European prestige (1956)
steps.page: Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal Company in July 1956; Britain, France and Israel invaded in October under a secretly agreed plan. American financial pressure and Soviet threats forced them out within weeks. The [crisis](event:suez-crisis) demonstrated in public that Britain and France could no longer act against Washington's wishes, and it was read across Africa and Asia as proof that the imperial powers could be faced down. Harold Macmillan's 'wind of change' speech in Cape Town followed less than four years later.

steps.name: The Year of Africa (1960)
steps.page: Seventeen African countries became independent during 1960, thirteen of them French: eight from French West Africa and five from French Equatorial Africa, along with Nigeria, Somalia, Madagascar and the Belgian Congo. Ghana had led the way in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah and Sudan in 1956. Congo's independence on 30 June was followed within weeks by mutiny, the secession of Katanga and a United Nations intervention, which showed how little the departing powers had left behind in the way of working administration.

steps.name: The end of the Portuguese empire (1974–1975)
steps.page: Portugal held on longest, fighting simultaneous wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau from 1961. The cost of them brought down the dictatorship at home: army officers overthrew the Estado Novo in the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974, and the new government withdrew. Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe and Angola all became independent in 1974–75. Angola and Mozambique went straight into civil wars in which the [Cold War](event:cold-war) powers, South Africa and Cuba all took part.

name: Independence of India and Pakistan
summary: British rule in South Asia ended in August 1947 and the subcontinent was divided into two independent states, India and Pakistan.
body:
Part of [Decolonisation](event:decolonisation). British rule in South Asia ended at midnight on 14–15 August 1947, and the subcontinent was divided into two independent dominions: India, with a Hindu majority, and Pakistan, with a Muslim one. Some 390 million people ceased to be British subjects. It was the largest single transfer of power in the history of the British Empire and one of the first steps in postwar [decolonisation](event:decolonisation).

It followed decades of mass campaigning by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League (non-cooperation from 1920, [the Salt March](event:salt-march) of 1930 and the Quit India movement of 1942) against an administration left financially and politically exhausted by the Second World War. The Labour government elected in Britain in 1945 accepted that withdrawal was unavoidable; the last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, brought the date forward by nearly a year.

[Partition](event:partition) came with it, and the two events are hard to separate: the boundary was published two days after independence, the migration and killing that followed displaced ten to twenty million people, and India and Pakistan were at war over Kashmir within months. Mohandas Gandhi, who had opposed partition, was assassinated in January 1948.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement).

name: Partition of India
summary: British India was split into India and Pakistan in August 1947, followed by mass migration and communal violence.
body:
Part of [Independence of India and Pakistan](event:indian-independence). Partition divided British India into two states in August 1947. The boundary through Punjab and Bengal was drawn by a commission under Cyril Radcliffe, an English lawyer who had never been to India, working from maps and census returns in about five weeks. The lines were published on 17 August, two days after independence.

Between ten and twenty million people moved, Hindus and Sikhs east into India and Muslims into the two wings of Pakistan, in the largest mass migration in recorded history. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to two million. Refugee columns and trains were attacked, villages were burned, and tens of thousands of women were abducted; the violence was worst in Punjab, where the line cut through a mixed and heavily armed population.

The princely states had to accede to one dominion or the other. Kashmir, with a Muslim majority and a Hindu ruler, hesitated, and the first India–Pakistan war followed within months. The line drawn there is still disputed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India).

name: The Cold War
summary: For more than four decades the United States and the Soviet Union confronted each other across the world without ever fighting each other directly.
body:
The Cold War was the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, and their respective blocs, that ran from the end of the Second World War to the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. It is called cold because the two never fought each other directly. They competed instead through alliances, arms, espionage, aid, propaganda and proxy wars in other countries.

The wartime alliance broke down over the future of Europe. The Soviet Union installed communist governments across the ground the Red Army had occupied; the United States answered with the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 and the [Marshall Plan](event:marshall-plan). The two blocs hardened into [NATO](event:nato-founded) in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955, with Germany, and Berlin inside it, the place where the line ran through a city.

Nuclear weapons made the confrontation unlike any before it. Both sides eventually held arsenals able to destroy the other several times over, and the resulting logic, that neither could attack without being destroyed in return, is usually credited with keeping them from war. It came closest to failing in October 1962 over [Cuba](event:cuban-missile-crisis).

Outside Europe the rivalry produced open wars. Korea, Vietnam, Angola, Central America and Afghanistan all saw wars in which one superpower or both armed a side, and both intervened in the internal politics of states across Asia, Africa and Latin America. The competition also ran through science, sport and prestige, most visibly in the [Space Race](event:space-race).

The confrontation ended between 1989 and 1991. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms after 1985 and his refusal to prop up the Eastern European governments by force led to their collapse in 1989, the [opening of the Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall) with them, and the [dissolution of the Soviet Union](event:soviet-collapse) on 26 December 1991.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War).

steps.name: The division of Europe (1947–1953)
steps.page: The confrontation took its shape in six years. President Truman told Congress in March 1947 that the United States would support free peoples resisting subjugation; the [Marshall Plan](event:marshall-plan) followed, and the Soviet Union forbade its satellites to join it. Communist parties took sole power in Poland, Hungary, Romania and, in February 1948, Czechoslovakia. The [Berlin blockade](event:berlin-blockade) of 1948–49 was the first direct trial of strength; [NATO](event:nato-founded) and two German states followed in 1949, the year the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb and the [Chinese Communists](event:prc-founded) won their civil war. The [Korean War](event:korean-war) from 1950 turned the rivalry into a worldwide military competition.

steps.name: Thaw and brink (1953–1962)
steps.page: Stalin died in March 1953 and the Korean armistice followed in July. Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin in 1956 and spoke of peaceful coexistence, but the same year Soviet tanks crushed the [Hungarian revolution](event:hungarian-revolution) and the [Suez crisis](event:suez-crisis) split the Western allies. [Sputnik](event:sputnik) in 1957 raised the fear of Soviet missiles and opened the [Space Race](event:space-race). East Germany sealed its border with the [Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall) in 1961, and the [Cuban Missile Crisis](event:cuban-missile-crisis) of October 1962 brought the two closest to nuclear war.

steps.name: Détente (1962–1979)
steps.page: After Cuba both sides looked for ways to manage the risk. A direct Moscow–Washington link was installed in 1963, along with a treaty banning atmospheric nuclear tests; the Non-Proliferation Treaty followed in 1968, SALT I and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty in 1972, and the Helsinki Final Act in 1975. Détente did not stop the [Vietnam War](event:vietnam-war), the crushing of the Prague Spring in 1968, or Soviet and American intervention in Africa and Latin America. It did make the rivalry a negotiated one, with agreed ceilings on weapons and rules for inspection.

steps.name: The Second Cold War (1979–1985)
steps.page: Relations broke down again at the end of the 1970s. The [Soviet invasion of Afghanistan](event:soviet-afghanistan) in December 1979 ended arms control; the United States boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics and the Soviet bloc the 1984 games in Los Angeles. Both sides deployed intermediate-range missiles in Europe, provoking the largest peace demonstrations of the period. Ronald Reagan increased American military spending sharply and announced a missile-defence programme in 1983, the year Soviet air defences shot down a Korean airliner and a NATO command exercise, Able Archer, was read in Moscow as a possible cover for attack. [Solidarity](event:solidarity-poland) in Poland was driven underground by martial law in 1981.

steps.name: Reform and collapse (1985–1991)
steps.page: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985 and set out to reform the system through glasnost and perestroika, while cutting the cost of confrontation abroad. He and Reagan signed the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty in 1987, the first to abolish a class of weapons, and Soviet troops left Afghanistan in 1989. Once Moscow made clear it would not intervene, the Eastern European governments fell in a few months of 1989, ending with the [opening of the Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall) in November. A failed hard-line coup in August 1991 destroyed what authority the centre had left, and the [Soviet Union dissolved](event:soviet-collapse) on 26 December.

name: Invention of the transistor
summary: Bell Labs built a solid-state amplifier and switch, the component from which all modern electronics is made.
body:
On 23 December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working in William Shockley's group at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, demonstrated the point-contact transistor: a small piece of germanium that could amplify and switch an electrical signal. It did the work of a vacuum tube with no heated filament, no vacuum and no glass envelope.

Shockley's junction transistor, worked out in 1948, was the design that could actually be manufactured, and silicon replaced germanium during the 1950s. The three men shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956. Transistors made hearing aids and pocket radios, then computers that did not fill a room and did not fail every few hours.

The next step was putting many of them on one piece of semiconductor: the integrated circuit, demonstrated by Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce in 1958–59, and then the [microprocessor](event:microprocessor) in 1971. The number of transistors on a chip has gone from one to tens of billions, which underlies modern computing, telecommunications and the [Internet](item:global-internet). The transistor is the most manufactured object in history.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transistor).

name: Marshall Plan
summary: American aid worth some $13 billion went to the reconstruction of Western Europe between 1948 and 1952.
body:
The Marshall Plan was an American programme of aid for the reconstruction of Western Europe. Secretary of State George Marshall proposed it in a speech at Harvard on 5 June 1947; Congress passed the Economic Cooperation Act on 3 April 1948, and about $13 billion (more than $150 billion in today's money) went to seventeen countries over the next four years.

Two years after the war Europe's currencies, harvests and industry were still broken, and the winter of 1946–47 had been severe. The aid came mostly as dollars to pay for imports (food, fuel, machinery and raw materials) rather than as loans to governments, and recipients had to agree among themselves on how it was divided, which was the beginning of European economic cooperation.

Industrial output in the recipient countries rose sharply, though economists still argue about how much of the recovery the money caused and how much it merely eased. The political effect is less disputed: the Soviet Union rejected the offer and required its satellites to refuse it too, so the plan drew across Europe the economic line that [NATO](event:nato-founded) drew militarily a year later. Its architects argued that rebuilding a defeated enemy worked better than the punitive settlement imposed after [the First World War](event:ww1), and West Germany was among the recipients.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Plan).

name: Founding of the State of Israel
summary: Israel declared independence as the British mandate ended; war with its Arab neighbours followed immediately, displacing some 700,000 Palestinians.
body:
David Ben-Gurion declared the establishment of the State of Israel in Tel Aviv on 14 May 1948, hours before the British Mandate for Palestine expired. Armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the country the next day. The war ran until armistices were signed during 1949.

The declaration followed the United Nations partition plan of November 1947, which proposed separate Jewish and Arab states with Jerusalem under international administration. Zionist leaders accepted it; Arab leaders rejected it, and fighting between the two communities in Palestine had already begun. Behind both stood the Zionist movement of the previous half century and the murder of European Jewry in [the Holocaust](event:holocaust).

Israel ended the war holding considerably more territory than the partition plan had allotted it. Some 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled and were not allowed to return, an event known in Arabic as the Nakba (catastrophe). No Palestinian state was established: the West Bank was annexed by Jordan and Gaza administered by Egypt. The dispute continued through the [Six-Day War](event:six-day-war), the [Camp David Accords](event:camp-david-accords) and the [war in Gaza](event:israel-hamas-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Declaration_of_Independence).

name: Berlin Blockade and Airlift
summary: The Soviets cut off West Berlin; Allied aircraft supplied the city for eleven months.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Soviet Union blockaded West Berlin from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949, cutting the road, rail and canal links between the western occupation zones of Germany and the western sectors of the city. The United States and Britain answered by flying supplies in. The airlift kept 2.2 million people fed and heated for eleven months, and the blockade was lifted without the Western powers leaving.

The immediate cause was currency reform: the Western allies introduced the Deutsche Mark in their zones in June 1948, which Moscow read as a move towards a separate West German state. Berlin lay about 160 kilometres inside the Soviet zone and was the obvious point at which to apply pressure.

Aircraft flew some 278,000 sorties and delivered about 2.3 million tonnes of cargo, most of it coal. At the peak an aircraft landed every few minutes; more than seventy airmen died in crashes. The crisis fixed West Berlin's status as a Western enclave, helped produce [NATO](event:nato-founded) in April 1949, and was followed within months by the founding of two German states. Berlin remained the sharpest point of the [Cold War](event:cold-war) until [the Wall](event:berlin-wall) went up in 1961.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Blockade).

name: NATO founded
summary: Twelve Western countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in 1949, creating a collective-defence alliance.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, creating a permanent military alliance between Western Europe and North America. Its centre is Article 5: an armed attack on one member is to be treated as an attack on all.

The treaty answered the Soviet consolidation of Eastern Europe and the [Berlin blockade](event:berlin-blockade), which was still running when it was signed. What was new was the American commitment to defend Europe in peacetime. An integrated command with an American supreme commander followed after the [Korean War](event:korean-war) began, and West Germany joined in 1955, which produced the Warsaw Pact in reply.

Article 5 has been invoked once, by the United States after [the attacks of 11 September 2001](event:9-11). After the [Cold War](event:cold-war) the alliance took in former Warsaw Pact states from 1999 and former Soviet republics from 2004, and Finland and Sweden joined after the [Russian invasion of Ukraine](event:ukraine-invasion), bringing the membership to 32. Its eastward expansion is one of the standing grievances of Russian foreign policy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO).

name: People's Republic of China proclaimed
summary: Mao Zedong declared the PRC from Tiananmen after the Communist victory in the civil war.
body:
Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China from the Gate of Heavenly Peace in Beijing on 1 October 1949. The Chinese Communist Party had won the civil war against the Kuomintang, whose government withdrew to Taiwan and continued to claim to rule all China, a dispute still unsettled.

The new state governed some 540 million people in a country wrecked by decades of war and invasion. Land was redistributed and landlords were tried and killed in large numbers; industry was nationalised; the Soviet Union supplied the model and, for a decade, the engineers. The Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 tried to industrialise at speed through collectivised agriculture and produced a famine in which tens of millions died.

The [Cultural Revolution](event:cultural-revolution) followed from 1966 until Mao's death in 1976. After 1978 Deng Xiaoping's reforms opened the economy to markets, private enterprise and foreign investment while the party kept its monopoly of political power, an arrangement reasserted by force at [Tiananmen Square](event:tiananmen-square) in 1989. Several hundred million people moved out of poverty, and China became the world's second-largest economy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China).

name: Green Revolution
summary: High-yielding dwarf wheat and rice, with fertiliser and irrigation, multiplied cereal harvests across Asia and Latin America between the 1940s and the 1970s.
body:
The Green Revolution was the spread of high-yielding cereal varieties, and of the fertiliser, irrigation and pesticides they need, through Latin America and Asia from the 1940s onwards. Wheat and rice yields in Mexico, India, Pakistan and the Philippines rose several-fold within a generation, and countries that had been expected to suffer mass famine became self-sufficient in grain.

The breeding was done first in Mexico, where the American agronomist Norman Borlaug developed semi-dwarf wheats: short-strawed, so that they carried heavy heads of grain without falling over, disease-resistant, and insensitive to day length, so that they could be grown at many latitudes. The International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines released IR8 rice on the same principle in 1966. India and Pakistan imported the wheats during the drought of 1965–66 and roughly doubled their harvests within five years.

Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970, and the programme is often credited with averting famine for hundreds of millions of people. It depended on nitrogen fertiliser, reliable water and machinery, and its costs have been argued over ever since: depleted aquifers, salinated and degraded soil, fertiliser run-off, loss of local crop varieties, and an advantage to farmers who could afford the inputs. It largely bypassed sub-Saharan Africa.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Revolution).

name: Korean War
summary: North Korea invaded the south in 1950; UN, Chinese and Korean armies fought to a stalemate near the original border, and the 1953 armistice has never become a peace treaty.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Korean War began when North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950 and ended with an armistice on 27 July 1953. The front finished close to where it had started. Between two and three million people died, most of them Korean civilians, and the peninsula is still divided along the line the fighting stopped on.

Korea had been split in 1945 into Soviet and American occupation zones, which hardened into two states in 1948, each claiming the whole. Stalin approved Kim Il-sung's plan to unify the country by force. The [United Nations](event:un-founded) Security Council authorised a military response (possible only because the Soviet delegate was boycotting the Council) and sixteen countries sent troops under American command.

It was the first war of the [Cold War](event:cold-war) fought between regular armies, and the confrontation became a global military one after it: American defence spending roughly tripled, [NATO](event:nato-founded) acquired an integrated command, and West German rearmament was put on the table. Neither Korea signed a peace treaty. The demilitarised zone remains one of the most heavily fortified borders in the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War).

steps.name: The invasion (June 1950)
steps.page: North Korean troops crossed the 38th parallel before dawn on 25 June 1950 with Soviet-supplied tanks and artillery. Seoul fell within three days. The Security Council called for the invasion to be repelled and President Truman committed American forces from Japan without asking Congress for a declaration of war.

steps.name: The Pusan perimeter (August–September)
steps.page: By August the South Korean and American forces had been pushed into the south-eastern corner of the peninsula around the port of Pusan. They held a perimeter roughly 230 kilometres long through six weeks of attacks while reinforcements and supplies arrived through the port.

steps.name: Inchon and the drive north (September–October)
steps.page: On 15 September General MacArthur landed X Corps at Inchon, far behind the North Korean army, against difficult tides and his own planners' advice. Seoul was retaken within two weeks and the North Korean army collapsed. UN forces crossed the 38th parallel and pushed towards the Yalu River on the Chinese border, past the war's original objective.

steps.name: China enters the war (October–January)
steps.page: China had warned that it would not accept hostile forces on the Yalu. Some 300,000 troops of the People's Volunteer Army crossed in October and attacked in force at the end of November, driving the UN armies back in the longest retreat in American military history. Seoul changed hands for the third time in January 1951. Truman dismissed MacArthur in April after he publicly pressed for war against China.

steps.name: Stalemate and armistice (1951–1953)
steps.page: From the summer of 1951 the front stabilised near the 38th parallel and the war became one of trenches, hills and heavy air bombardment. Armistice talks opened on 10 July 1951 at Kaesong, moved to Panmunjom, and dragged on for two years, mostly over whether prisoners who did not want to go home had to be repatriated. The armistice signed on 27 July 1953 fixed the line where the fighting had stopped and created a demilitarised zone about four kilometres wide across the peninsula. No peace treaty has followed it.

name: Structure of DNA
summary: Watson and Crick, using Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data, described the double helix and with it how genes are copied.
body:
James Watson and Francis Crick published the structure of DNA in *Nature* on 25 April 1953. Two chains wind in opposite directions around a common axis, with the bases paired in the middle: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. The pairing rule immediately suggested how genetic material is copied: separate the two strands, and each specifies the other.

The model was built at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, largely from X-ray diffraction data produced at King's College London by Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling, in particular the image known as Photograph 51, which Maurice Wilkins showed to Watson without Franklin's knowledge. Erwin Chargaff's measurements, showing that adenine and thymine occurred in equal amounts and so did guanine and cytosine, were the other essential clue. Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared the Nobel Prize in 1962; Franklin had died of ovarian cancer in 1958, and the prize is not awarded posthumously.

The structure founded molecular biology. The genetic code was deciphered during the 1960s, recombinant DNA followed in the 1970s, and [the Human Genome Project](event:human-genome) and [CRISPR](event:crispr) descend directly from it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleic_acid_double_helix).

name: American civil rights movement
summary: A mass campaign of litigation, boycotts and marches ended legal segregation and disenfranchisement in the United States between 1954 and 1968.
body:
The civil rights movement was the campaign to end legal racial segregation, discrimination and disenfranchisement in the United States. It is usually dated from the Supreme Court's ruling against segregated schooling in 1954 to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. and the fair housing law of 1968. Its methods were litigation, boycotts, marches and deliberate breaches of segregation laws, and it produced three federal statutes that dismantled the system known as Jim Crow.

Segregation in the southern states rested on state laws upheld by the Supreme Court in 1896, and on the poll taxes, literacy tests and violence that kept most black southerners off the electoral roll. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People had been attacking those laws in the courts since the 1930s; from the mid-1950s it was joined by church-based and student organisations (the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and the Congress of Racial Equality) which took the argument into the streets.

Nonviolent confrontation was a tactic as well as a principle: televised pictures of police dogs, fire hoses and beatings in Birmingham and Selma moved opinion outside the South and made federal action possible. Resistance was severe, and activists were beaten, jailed and killed. The [Civil Rights Act](event:civil-rights-act) of 1964 outlawed segregation in employment and public accommodation, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 put federal registrars behind the ballot, and the Fair Housing Act followed a week after [King's murder](event:mlk-assassination) in 1968.

The movement's later years turned north, where segregation was a matter of housing, schooling and policing rather than of law, and where progress was slower; younger activists argued for Black Power and against King's insistence on nonviolence. Legal equality was won; disparities in wealth, imprisonment and life expectancy were not closed, and remain a subject of American politics. The stages of the campaign are the steps of this saga.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement).

steps.name: Brown v. Board of Education (1954)
steps.page: On 17 May 1954 the Supreme Court held unanimously in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal, overturning the doctrine of "separate but equal" it had approved in 1896. The ruling did not set a deadline; a second decision in 1955 asked for desegregation "with all deliberate speed", and southern states organised a campaign of massive resistance that kept most schools segregated for another decade.

steps.name: The Montgomery bus boycott (1955–1956)
steps.page: Rosa Parks, a seamstress and NAACP secretary, was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama on 1 December 1955 for refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger. Black residents boycotted the city's buses for 381 days, walking or sharing cars, and chose a 26-year-old minister, Martin Luther King Jr., to lead the association that ran it. The Supreme Court struck down Alabama's bus segregation laws in November 1956 and the boycott ended on 20 December.

steps.name: Sit-ins and Freedom Rides (1960–1961)
steps.page: Four students sat at a segregated lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina on 1 February 1960 and refused to leave. Sit-ins spread to dozens of cities within weeks and produced the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality sent integrated groups of Freedom Riders through the South to test a court ruling against segregated interstate travel; buses were burned and riders beaten in Alabama, and federal marshals were sent in. The Interstate Commerce Commission ordered desegregated terminals from November 1961.

steps.name: The Birmingham campaign (1963)
steps.page: From April 1963 the Southern Christian Leadership Conference concentrated on Birmingham, Alabama, one of the most rigidly segregated cities in the country. King was arrested and wrote his "Letter from Birmingham Jail"; in May the campaign put schoolchildren on the streets, and the city's police commissioner Eugene "Bull" Connor answered with dogs and fire hoses in front of the television cameras. The pictures shocked national opinion, an agreement desegregated the city's stores, and President Kennedy proposed the civil rights bill in June.

steps.name: Selma and the Voting Rights Act (1965)
steps.page: Marchers leaving Selma, Alabama for the state capital on 7 March 1965 were beaten by state troopers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge, a day known as "Bloody Sunday", and the third attempt, protected by federalised troops, reached Montgomery on 25 March. President Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act on 6 August 1965, suspending literacy tests and sending federal examiners to register voters in the states with the worst records. Black registration in the Deep South rose sharply within a few years.

steps.name: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.

name: Polio vaccine developed
summary: Jonas Salk's polio vaccine was declared safe and effective in 1955 after the largest medical field trial then attempted, and epidemic polio soon disappeared from the wealthy world.
body:
The Salk polio vaccine was declared safe and effective on 12 April 1955, after a field trial involving some 1.8 million American schoolchildren, the largest medical trial attempted to that date. Mass immunisation began at once. Paralytic polio in the United States fell from tens of thousands of cases a year to fewer than a hundred within a decade.

Poliomyelitis is caused by a virus that usually produces a mild illness but occasionally attacks the nervous system, paralysing limbs or the muscles used to breathe. Epidemics grew worse through the first half of the twentieth century in wealthy countries with good sanitation, where children met the virus later in life and with less protection from maternal antibodies. Wards of iron lungs were used to keep paralysed patients breathing.

Salk's vaccine uses inactivated virus and is injected. Albert Sabin's live attenuated vaccine, licensed from 1961, is given by mouth, costs less and spreads immunity to contacts; it became the basis of the global eradication campaign launched by the World Health Organization in 1988, which has cut cases by more than 99 per cent. Wild poliovirus remains endemic only in Afghanistan and Pakistan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polio_vaccine).

name: The Space Race
summary: The United States and the Soviet Union competed for two decades to reach orbit and then the Moon, in a contest of prestige built on missile technology.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Space Race was the competition between the United States and the Soviet Union in spaceflight, running from rival announcements of satellite programmes in 1955 to the joint Apollo–Soyuz docking of 1975. The Soviet Union led at the start, launching the first satellite, the first man and the first woman into space; the United States answered with the Apollo programme and landed the first crew on the Moon in 1969.

Both programmes grew out of ballistic missile development, and both used rockets designed to carry warheads. That is why [Sputnik 1](event:sputnik) alarmed Washington in October 1957: a satellite in orbit meant a missile that could reach North America. The response was the creation of NASA in 1958, a large increase in federal spending on science education, and, after [Yuri Gagarin's flight](event:gagarin) in April 1961, President Kennedy's commitment to land a man on the Moon before the end of the decade.

The Soviet effort rested heavily on one chief designer, Sergei Korolev, whose death in 1966 left the lunar programme without its organiser; the giant N1 rocket failed on all four of its test launches and the Soviet Union never attempted a crewed flight to the Moon. The [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program) put twelve men on the surface between 1969 and 1972.

Competition gave way to cooperation. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 barred national appropriation of the Moon and weapons of mass destruction in orbit, and in July 1975 an Apollo capsule docked with a Soyuz spacecraft in orbit, which most accounts take as the end of the race. The programmes left behind the satellite infrastructure used for communications, navigation and weather forecasting. The milestones are the steps of this saga.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Race).

steps.name: The satellite announcements (1955–1957)
steps.page: The United States announced on 29 July 1955 that it would launch an artificial satellite during the International Geophysical Year; the Soviet Union said within days that it would do the same. The American effort was given to the civilian Vanguard project rather than to the army rocket team under Wernher von Braun, partly to keep the satellite programme separate from the missile programme. The Soviet team under Sergei Korolev adapted the R-7 intercontinental missile and got there first.

steps.name: Explorer 1 and the founding of NASA (1958)
steps.page: After the Vanguard rocket exploded on the pad in December 1957, von Braun's team was allowed to try, and Explorer 1 reached orbit on 31 January 1958 carrying the instrument that found the Van Allen radiation belts. Congress created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, a civilian agency, in July 1958; it began work on 1 October. The Advanced Research Projects Agency, later the parent of [ARPANET](event:internet), was founded in the same reorganisation.

steps.name: The Soviet lunar programme (1966–1974)
steps.page: Korolev died during surgery in January 1966 and the Soviet effort lost the man who had held its rival design bureaux together. The N1 rocket built for a lunar landing failed on all four test launches between 1969 and 1972, the second destroying its launch complex. The Soviet Union flew uncrewed sample-return missions and the Lunokhod rovers instead, cancelled the crewed programme, and turned to long-duration flight in the Salyut space stations.

steps.name: Apollo–Soyuz (1975)
steps.page: An Apollo command module and a Soyuz spacecraft docked in orbit on 17 July 1975 using a jointly designed adapter, and the crews of Thomas Stafford and Alexei Leonov exchanged visits, gifts and a handshake broadcast live. It was the first international crewed mission, the last flight of an Apollo spacecraft, and is usually taken as the end of the Space Race. Joint work resumed in the 1990s with Shuttle–Mir and the International Space Station.

name: Vietnam War
summary: A twenty-year war in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia that drew in the United States, ended with its withdrawal in 1973, and left Vietnam unified under the communist north.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Vietnam War was fought from 1955 to 1975 between North Vietnam and its southern allies, the Viet Cong, and the government of South Vietnam, which was supported from 1965 by American combat forces. It spread into Laos and Cambodia. Estimates of the dead range from about one million to three million Vietnamese, most of them civilians, along with some 58,000 Americans; the war ended when North Vietnamese forces took Saigon on 30 April 1975.

Vietnam had been partitioned at the seventeenth parallel by the Geneva Accords of 1954, which ended French rule after the defeat at Dien Bien Phu and promised elections that were never held. The United States backed the anti-communist government in the south, first with advisers and money and, after the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964, with ground troops and a sustained bombing campaign. American strength peaked at about 540,000 men in 1969. The Soviet Union and China supplied the north.

It was a war without a front. Guerrilla warfare, search-and-destroy operations, defoliants such as Agent Orange, and more bomb tonnage than was dropped in the whole of the Second World War failed to break the north's willingness to continue. The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a military defeat for the communist forces, but it shifted opinion in the United States, where the war was reported nightly on television and opposed by a large protest movement.

American troops were withdrawn under the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 and the south fell two years later. Vietnam was formally reunified in 1976. The war left the country damaged and heavily mined and produced millions of refugees. The concurrent wars in Laos and Cambodia ended with the Khmer Rouge taking power in Cambodia in 1975. Its phases are the steps of this saga.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War).

steps.name: Partition and the advisers (1955–1963)
steps.page: The Geneva Accords of July 1954 divided Vietnam at the seventeenth parallel pending elections. Ngo Dinh Diem, who refused to hold them, declared the Republic of Vietnam in October 1955; the north supported a growing southern insurgency, organised from 1960 as the National Liberation Front. The United States sent advisers, aircraft and money (about 16,000 advisers by 1963) and supported the generals who overthrew and killed Diem on 2 November 1963.

steps.name: The Gulf of Tonkin (1964)
steps.page: American destroyers reported attacks by North Vietnamese torpedo boats in the Gulf of Tonkin on 2 and 4 August 1964; the second engagement is now generally held not to have taken place. Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution on 7 August, authorising President Johnson to use armed force in Southeast Asia without a declaration of war. It was the legal basis of American escalation for the next seven years.

steps.name: Escalation (1965–1967)
steps.page: Operation Rolling Thunder, a bombing campaign against the north, began in March 1965, and the first Marine battalions landed at Da Nang days later. American strength grew from about 23,000 to more than 480,000 men by the end of 1967. The strategy was attrition, measured in body counts, pursued through search-and-destroy operations in the countryside, while the north moved supplies south along the Ho Chi Minh Trail through Laos and Cambodia.

steps.name: The Tet Offensive (1968)
steps.page: On the lunar new year of 30 January 1968 communist forces attacked more than a hundred towns and cities across the south at once, including the American embassy in Saigon, and held the old capital of Hue for a month. Militarily the offensive failed and the Viet Cong lost much of its strength. Politically it was decisive: it contradicted official claims that the war was being won, President Johnson withdrew from the presidential race in March, and Washington began to look for a way out.

steps.name: Vietnamisation and Cambodia (1969–1972)
steps.page: President Nixon began withdrawing American troops in 1969 while transferring the ground war to the South Vietnamese army and intensifying the bombing, which was extended to Cambodia and Laos. The incursion into Cambodia in 1970 set off the largest protests of the war in the United States, where four students were shot dead at Kent State. The north's Easter Offensive of 1972 was halted with American air power, and negotiations in Paris reached a settlement in October.

steps.name: The Paris Peace Accords (1973)
steps.page: The agreement signed in Paris on 27 January 1973 provided for a ceasefire, the withdrawal of all American forces within sixty days and the return of prisoners of war, while leaving North Vietnamese troops in place in the south. The last American combat troops left in March. Congress cut military aid to Saigon and, in the War Powers Resolution of November 1973, restricted the president's freedom to commit forces abroad.

steps.name: The fall of Saigon (1975)
steps.page: North Vietnam opened a general offensive in March 1975. The southern army collapsed faster than either side expected, abandoning the central highlands and then the coastal cities. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, with the last Americans and some of their Vietnamese staff lifted by helicopter from the embassy compound the day before. Vietnam was formally reunified as a single republic in July 1976.

name: Suez Crisis
summary: Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal; Britain, France and Israel invaded, and American and Soviet pressure forced them to withdraw.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal Company in July 1956. Britain, France and Israel invaded in October under a plan agreed in secret, and were forced to withdraw within weeks by American financial pressure and Soviet threats. The affair is usually taken as the moment Britain and France ceased to be independent great powers.

Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the company on 26 July, after the United States and Britain withdrew funding for the Aswan High Dam. The canal was owned by British and French shareholders and carried much of Western Europe's oil. At Sèvres the three governments agreed that Israel would attack across Sinai and that Britain and France would then intervene as peacekeepers to separate the combatants and occupy the canal zone.

Israel attacked on 29 October and Anglo-French forces landed at Port Said on 5 November. President Eisenhower, who had not been consulted, refused to support sterling until Britain agreed to a ceasefire; the Soviet Union, then busy crushing the [Hungarian revolution](event:hungarian-revolution), threatened rocket attacks. A United Nations force took over and the invaders left by December.

Anthony Eden resigned as British prime minister in January 1957. Nasser's standing across the Arab world rose sharply, and the [Cold War](event:cold-war) superpowers replaced the old imperial powers as the outside forces in the Middle East.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis).

name: Hungarian Revolution
summary: A national uprising ended Soviet-imposed rule in Hungary for ten days; Soviet forces returned on 4 November 1956 and suppressed it.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). A student demonstration in Budapest on 23 October 1956 grew within days into a national uprising against Soviet-imposed communist rule. A reform government under Imre Nagy took office, ended the one-party system and declared Hungary neutral and out of the Warsaw Pact. Soviet armour returned in force on 4 November and crushed the revolt.

The revolution followed months of loosening after Khrushchev's denunciation of Stalin in February. Crowds pulled down the Stalin statue in Budapest, secret police were killed in the street, and workers' councils and a free press appeared in a fortnight. Soviet troops withdrew from the capital at the end of October, which was read at the time as a victory.

Some 2,500 Hungarians and 700 Soviet soldiers were killed in the fighting; around 200,000 people left the country, and Nagy was tried in secret and executed in 1958. The revolt coincided with the [Suez crisis](event:suez-crisis), which occupied the Western powers, and no help came. Moscow had shown that it would use the army to hold its sphere; it did so again in Czechoslovakia in 1968, and the policy changed only under Gorbachev.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1956).

name: Sputnik 1
summary: The first artificial satellite circled the Earth every 96 minutes; its launch set off a large American response.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, on 4 October 1957 from the Baikonur site in Kazakhstan. It was a polished metal sphere 58 centimetres across with four trailing antennas, weighing 84 kilograms, and it circled the Earth every 96 minutes on an elliptical orbit, transmitting a radio pulse that amateur operators anywhere could pick up.

The satellite carried no instruments beyond a thermometer and a pressure gauge; its purpose was to be there. It was launched by an adapted R-7 intercontinental ballistic missile, which is what gave it its military meaning: a rocket that could put a payload in orbit could deliver a warhead to another continent. Its batteries lasted three weeks and it burned up on re-entry in January 1958.

In the United States the launch produced what was called the Sputnik crisis. Congress increased federal spending on science and mathematics teaching through the National Defense Education Act, the Advanced Research Projects Agency was set up, and NASA was created as a civilian space agency in 1958. The first American satellite, Explorer 1, reached orbit that January.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sputnik_1).

name: Fidel Castro takes power in Cuba
summary: Fidel Castro's guerrillas overthrew the Batista dictatorship on 1 January 1959; within two years Cuba was a one-party socialist state allied with the Soviet Union.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista on 1 January 1959, when Batista fled the country after his army failed to hold Santa Clara. Castro's forces entered Havana a week later. Within two years Cuba had nationalised American property, declared itself socialist and become the Soviet Union's ally ninety miles from Florida.

The revolt began with a failed attack on the Moncada barracks in July 1953, for which Castro was jailed and then exiled. He returned from Mexico in December 1956 aboard the yacht Granma with about eighty men; most were killed or captured within days, and the survivors, among them Che Guevara and Raúl Castro, waged a guerrilla war from the Sierra Maestra mountains while urban networks struck in the cities. Batista's summer offensive of 1958 failed, and his government, which had lost American arms supplies under an embargo, collapsed at the end of the year.

The new government redistributed land, expropriated foreign-owned sugar mills and utilities, and tried and executed hundreds of Batista's officials. The United States answered with a trade embargo and, in April 1961, the failed Bay of Pigs landing by Cuban exiles; the following year Soviet missiles on the island brought the [Cuban Missile Crisis](event:cuban-missile-crisis). Cuba built health and education systems with indicators above the regional average, and a one-party state that jailed dissidents; hundreds of thousands emigrated. Castro governed until 2008, when he handed power to his brother.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Revolution).

name: Berlin Wall built
summary: East Germany walled off West Berlin overnight to stop the flight of its population.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). East Germany sealed the border around West Berlin on the night of 13 August 1961, first with barbed wire and then with a concrete wall. The barrier ran about 155 kilometres around the western sectors of the city and stood for 28 years, until it was opened on 9 November 1989.

It was built to stop emigration. Berlin was the one place where East Germans could walk into the West, and some 2.7 million had left the country since 1949, disproportionately the young and the qualified. The wall closed that route overnight, cutting streets, tram lines and families in two.

Behind the wall on the eastern side lay a death strip of raked sand, watchtowers, floodlights and patrols, with orders to shoot anyone attempting to cross. At least 140 people were killed at the Berlin Wall, and several hundred more died along the inner-German border. Others got through by tunnel, hot-air balloon, forged papers or hidden compartments in cars.

In the West the wall was used as an illustration of the [Cold War](event:cold-war) division of Europe. Kennedy spoke at the Schöneberg town hall in 1963 and Reagan at the Brandenburg Gate in 1987; its [opening](event:berlin-wall-fall) in 1989 became an image of the end of communist rule in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall).

name: Yuri Gagarin orbits the Earth
summary: The first human in space completed a single orbit aboard Vostok 1 and landed by parachute.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). Yuri Gagarin became the first human being to travel into space on 12 April 1961, aboard the Soviet spacecraft Vostok 1. He completed a single orbit of the Earth in about 108 minutes, reaching a maximum altitude of some 327 kilometres, and landed by parachute in the Saratov region after ejecting from the descending capsule at about seven kilometres.

Gagarin was a 27-year-old air force pilot, the son of a carpenter and a dairy farmer, chosen from a group of twenty partly for his size, since the Vostok cabin was small. The flight was automatic, with the controls locked against the possibility that weightlessness would leave a pilot unable to think clearly; he carried an envelope with the unlocking code in case of emergency.

The flight was announced only after it had succeeded and was a considerable propaganda victory: the Soviet Union had put a man in orbit while the United States was preparing a suborbital hop, which Alan Shepard flew three weeks later. It is one of the reasons President Kennedy chose the Moon as the target where the American programme could hope to arrive first. Gagarin never flew in space again and was killed in a training jet crash in 1968; 12 April is marked as Cosmonautics Day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Gagarin).

name: Apollo programme
summary: The American programme that landed twelve men on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, begun by Kennedy's commitment to do it before the decade was out.
body:
Part of [The Space Race](event:space-race). Apollo was the American programme that carried crews to the Moon. President Kennedy set its goal before Congress on 25 May 1961, to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the decade was out, and it was met on 20 July 1969. Six missions landed between 1969 and 1972 and twelve men walked on the surface; the programme ended with Apollo 17 in December 1972.

It was run by NASA and at its peak employed some 400,000 people across government, universities and contractors, taking a little over 4 per cent of the federal budget in 1966. Its instrument was the Saturn V, a rocket 110 metres tall, and a mission plan (lunar orbit rendezvous) in which a small lander separated from the mothership in orbit around the Moon and returned to it afterwards. The programme also drove work on fuel cells, integrated circuits and software engineering.

Progress was neither smooth nor cheap. Three astronauts died in a fire on the launch pad in 1967, and [Apollo 13](event:apollo-13) came near to being lost in 1970. Public support fell once the goal had been reached; the last three planned missions were cancelled on cost grounds, and the hardware built for them went to museums and to the Skylab station.

The missions returned 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, left instrument packages that measured moonquakes and the Moon's distance for years afterwards, and produced the photographs (Earthrise and the Blue Marble) that became emblems of the environmental movement. No one has been beyond low Earth orbit since 1972. The flights are the steps of this saga.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_program).

steps.name: The Apollo 1 fire (1967)
steps.page: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee were killed on 27 January 1967 when fire broke out in their command module during a rehearsal on the launch pad at Cape Kennedy. The cabin was pressurised with pure oxygen, the hatch opened inwards and could not be released in time, and the interior was full of flammable material. Crewed flights stopped for twenty months while the spacecraft was redesigned; most accounts hold that the pause is what made the later landings possible.

steps.name: Apollo 8 orbits the Moon (1968)
steps.page: Apollo 8 launched on 21 December 1968 and became the first crewed spacecraft to leave Earth orbit, reach the Moon and return. Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and William Anders made ten orbits on Christmas Eve, read from the book of Genesis in a broadcast heard by a very large audience, and photographed the Earth rising over the lunar horizon. The mission was brought forward partly out of concern that the Soviet Union was preparing a circumlunar flight.

steps.name: Apollo 17 and the end of the programme (1972)
steps.page: The last Apollo mission launched on 7 December 1972 and splashed down on 19 December. Eugene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt (the only professional geologist to reach the Moon) spent three days in the Taurus–Littrow valley, drove the lunar rover some 36 kilometres and collected the largest sample return of the programme. Apollo 18, 19 and 20 had already been cancelled. Cernan was the last person to stand on the Moon.

name: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Thirteen days in October 1962, after Soviet nuclear missiles were found in Cuba, brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other moment.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Cuban Missile Crisis was a thirteen-day confrontation in October 1962 between the United States and the Soviet Union over Soviet nuclear missiles installed in Cuba. It is generally regarded as the closest the [Cold War](event:cold-war) came to nuclear war. It ended with the missiles withdrawn in exchange for an American undertaking not to invade Cuba and a private agreement to remove American missiles from Turkey.

American U-2 photographs on 14 October 1962 showed launch sites under construction for medium-range ballistic missiles able to reach much of the continental United States. Moscow's motives are usually given as the defence of [Castro's Cuba](event:castro-cuba) after the Bay of Pigs landing and the correction of a large imbalance in intercontinental missiles, with the American Jupiters in Turkey and Italy as the precedent.

President Kennedy chose a naval quarantine of the island over an air strike, and announced it in a television address on 22 October. Soviet ships turned back at the line; the crisis peaked on 27 October, when a U-2 was shot down over Cuba and a Soviet submarine commander under depth-charge attack considered using a nuclear torpedo. Khrushchev announced the withdrawal of the missiles on 28 October.

Both leaders were criticised at home for conceding, and the Turkish half of the bargain was kept secret for decades. A direct Moscow–Washington teleprinter link followed in 1963, along with the Partial Test Ban Treaty, and the crisis is the standard case study in the management of nuclear risk.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban_Missile_Crisis).

name: Assassination of John F. Kennedy
summary: President Kennedy was shot while riding through Dallas in an open car, and Vice-President Lyndon Johnson was sworn in the same afternoon.
body:
President John F. Kennedy was shot and killed in Dallas, Texas, on 22 November 1963, while riding through Dealey Plaza in an open car. Governor John Connally, sitting in front of him, was seriously wounded. Vice-President Lyndon Johnson was sworn in aboard the presidential aircraft the same afternoon.

Lee Harvey Oswald, a warehouse employee who had lived in the Soviet Union and returned, was arrested within ninety minutes, having also shot a Dallas police officer. Two days later, while being moved between jails in front of television cameras, he was shot dead by a nightclub owner named Jack Ruby. The Warren Commission reported in 1964 that Oswald had acted alone; a House committee concluded in 1979 that a conspiracy was likely, on acoustic evidence later discredited. Polls have consistently found that most Americans do not accept the lone-gunman finding, and the assassination has generated a very large literature.

The killing was the first to be experienced as a live national event on television, and the amateur film shot by Abraham Zapruder is among the most examined pieces of footage ever made. Johnson used the aftermath to push through Kennedy's stalled legislation, including the [Civil Rights Act](event:civil-rights-act) of 1964, and went on to escalate [the war in Vietnam](event:vietnam-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_John_F._Kennedy).

name: March on Washington
summary: A quarter of a million people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to hear King's "I Have a Dream" speech.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom brought about a quarter of a million people to the Lincoln Memorial on 28 August 1963. It was organised by a coalition of civil rights, labour and religious groups to demand civil rights legislation, an end to school segregation, protection from police brutality and a federal jobs programme with a minimum wage.

The organisers were A. Philip Randolph, who had proposed a similar march in 1941, and Bayard Rustin, who put it together in two months. The Kennedy administration, which had a civil rights bill before Congress, tried first to have it called off and then worked to keep it orderly. It was one of the largest political gatherings the capital had seen, and it passed without disorder.

Martin Luther King Jr. spoke last, and departed from his prepared text for the passage beginning "I have a dream", which was broadcast live and became the best-known American speech of the century. The march is generally credited with helping to secure the [Civil Rights Act](event:civil-rights-act) of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_on_Washington_for_Jobs_and_Freedom).

name: The Beatles rise to global fame
summary: Four musicians from Liverpool became the most popular band in the world in the mid-1960s and changed how popular music was made and heard.
body:
The Beatles (John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr) were an English rock band formed in Liverpool in 1960. They became the most commercially successful and widely imitated act in popular music, and their arrival in the United States in February 1964 was followed by the British Invasion of the American charts.

The group served an apprenticeship in Liverpool clubs and in Hamburg before signing to EMI's Parlophone label in 1962 with the producer George Martin. "Love Me Do" and "Please Please Me" made them famous in Britain during 1963, and the press named the crowds that followed them Beatlemania. Their appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964 was watched by an audience estimated at 73 million, and led the British Invasion of American charts.

They stopped touring in 1966 and worked in the studio, where multitrack recording, tape manipulation and unconventional instrumentation produced Revolver, Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band and the White Album. Those records helped establish the album, rather than the single, as the unit of popular music, and songwriting by performers as the norm.

The band broke up in 1970 after eight years of recording. They remain the best-selling music act in history, and their recordings are closely associated with the youth culture of the 1960s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles).

name: Civil Rights Act of 1964
summary: Federal law outlawed discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin in employment and public accommodation.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination on grounds of race, colour, religion, sex or national origin. President Johnson signed it on 2 July 1964. It ended lawful segregation in public accommodation (hotels, restaurants, theatres and transport) and in employment, and it is the foundation of American anti-discrimination law.

Kennedy had proposed the bill in June 1963, after the police response to the Birmingham campaign, and it was still in committee when he was killed. Johnson made it his first legislative priority. Southern senators filibustered for 60 working days, the longest in Senate history to that point; it was broken in June 1964 with Republican votes led by Everett Dirksen.

The act let the federal government withhold funds from public bodies that discriminated and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to investigate complaints. The prohibition of sex discrimination was added late, by a southern congressman, and became one of the act's most far-reaching provisions. Voting rights were left largely untouched and were addressed by the Voting Rights Act the following year. Johnson is said to have remarked that the Democratic Party had lost the South for a generation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964).

name: Cultural Revolution
summary: Mao mobilised students against the party and the "four olds"; universities closed, millions were persecuted and much cultural heritage was destroyed.
body:
Part of [People's Republic of China proclaimed](event:prc-founded). The Cultural Revolution was a mass political movement launched by Mao Zedong in May 1966 and ended by his death in September 1976. Its stated purpose was to purge capitalist and traditional elements from Chinese society and to restore revolutionary purity; in practice it was also Mao's attack on rivals in the Communist Party who had sidelined him after the famine of the Great Leap Forward.

Students formed Red Guard units and were told to attack the "four olds": old customs, culture, habits and ideas. Party officials, teachers, writers and anyone with foreign or landowning connections were denounced at struggle sessions, beaten, imprisoned or driven to suicide. Universities closed for years and schooling was disrupted for a generation; some 17 million young people were later sent to work in the countryside. Temples, monasteries, libraries and artworks were destroyed.

Factional fighting between Red Guard groups became armed in 1967, and the army was used to restore order. Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, died in detention in 1969. Lin Biao, named as Mao's successor, died in an air crash in 1971 fleeing after an alleged plot. Power in the final years lay with the group later called the Gang of Four, arrested weeks after Mao's death.

Estimates of the death toll range from several hundred thousand to a few million, and many millions more were persecuted. The Communist Party's own verdict, adopted in 1981, called the decade responsible for the most severe setback suffered by the country since 1949. Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms followed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution).

name: Six-Day War
summary: Israel decisively defeated Egypt, Syria and Jordan in six days, occupying the West Bank, Gaza Strip and Golan Heights.
body:
Israel fought Egypt, Jordan and Syria between 5 and 10 June 1967 and defeated all three. It opened with a surprise air strike that destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground, and ended with Israel holding the Sinai peninsula, the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, three times the territory it had held a week earlier.

The crisis built through May 1967, when Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser moved troops into Sinai, expelled the United Nations force stationed there since [Suez](event:suez-crisis) and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping, which Israel had said it would treat as an act of war. Jordan placed its army under Egyptian command. Whether the Israeli strike is best described as pre-emptive or as a war of choice remains disputed.

Around 20,000 Arab and about 800 Israeli soldiers were killed. Some 300,000 Palestinians and 100,000 Syrians left the occupied territories. More than a million Palestinians came under Israeli military government, and Jewish settlement in the occupied territories began within months.

Security Council Resolution 242 of November 1967 called for withdrawal from territories occupied in the conflict in exchange for recognition and peace, the formula behind every negotiation since, including the [Camp David Accords](event:camp-david-accords), which returned Sinai to Egypt. The occupation of the West Bank and Gaza has never been settled.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six-Day_War).

name: First successful human heart transplant
summary: Christiaan Barnard in Cape Town transplanted a donor heart into a patient who survived for 18 days, proving transplantation possible.
body:
Christiaan Barnard and his team at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town carried out the first human-to-human heart transplant on 3 December 1967. The patient, Louis Washkansky, was a 53-year-old grocer dying of heart failure; the donor was Denise Darvall, a young woman fatally injured by a car. The transplanted heart worked, and Washkansky lived for eighteen days before dying of pneumonia.

The operation was made possible by a decade of experimental work on cardiac surgery and by the heart-lung machine, and it depended on drugs that suppressed rejection of the graft, the same drugs that left the patient unable to fight infection. That was the central problem: the technique was surgically feasible before it was survivable.

The publicity was enormous and about a hundred transplants were attempted worldwide within a year, most of them with poor results; many centres abandoned the procedure. It became a routine treatment only after the introduction of ciclosporin around 1980, better tissue matching and standardised criteria for brain death, which the transplant era itself forced medicine and the law to define. Several thousand heart transplants are now performed each year, with most recipients surviving well beyond a decade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_transplantation).

name: Assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
summary: King was shot in Memphis while supporting a strike by sanitation workers; riots followed in over a hundred cities.
body:
Part of [American civil rights movement](event:civil-rights). Martin Luther King Jr. was shot dead on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee on 4 April 1968. He was 39, and had come to the city to support a strike by its black sanitation workers. He had led the movement against segregation since the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955 and had received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

James Earl Ray, an escaped convict, was arrested in London two months later, pleaded guilty in 1969 and was sentenced to 99 years. He recanted his plea days afterwards and died in prison in 1998. A House committee concluded in 1979 that Ray had fired the shot but that a conspiracy was likely, and members of King's family later said publicly that they did not accept the official account.

Riots followed in more than a hundred American cities in the days after the killing, with dozens of deaths and troops deployed in Washington, Baltimore and Chicago. Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, banning discrimination in the sale and rental of housing, a week later. King's last campaign, the Poor People's Campaign against economic inequality, went ahead without him; a federal holiday in his name was first observed in 1986.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Martin_Luther_King_Jr.).

name: Stonewall uprising
summary: Police raided a gay bar in Greenwich Village in June 1969; the customers and the crowd resisted, and the riots are generally treated as the start of the modern gay rights movement.
body:
Police raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar on Christopher Street in Greenwich Village, New York, in the early hours of 28 June 1969. Raids on such bars were routine; this time the customers and the crowd outside fought back, and the confrontations continued around the street for several nights. Stonewall is generally treated as the beginning of the modern gay rights movement.

Homosexual acts were illegal in almost every American state, bars serving gay customers could lose their licences, and the police used loitering and cross-dressing laws to make arrests.
