The Stonewall's patrons included drag queens, transgender women, homeless young people and hustlers. Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, both later prominent activists, were among those present.

Existing homophile groups had campaigned quietly for years; the organisations formed within weeks of the riot, notably the Gay Liberation Front, were louder and more confrontational. On the first anniversary, 28 June 1970, marches in New York, Los Angeles and Chicago became the first Pride parades, now held in cities around the world.

The movement that followed won decriminalisation, the removal of homosexuality from the American psychiatric manual in 1973, anti-discrimination law and eventually [marriage rights](event:usa-marriage-equality). The Stonewall Inn and the park opposite were designated a national monument in 2016.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonewall_riots).

name: The Troubles begin in Northern Ireland
summary: Civil rights marches by Northern Ireland’s Catholic minority met violence, and the province entered three decades of sectarian conflict.
body:
The Troubles were a conflict in Northern Ireland that ran from the late 1960s to 1998. They are usually dated from August 1969, when rioting in Derry and Belfast overwhelmed the police and British troops were sent onto the streets. About 3,500 people were killed over the following thirty years, more than half of them civilians.

The dispute was constitutional: unionists, mostly Protestant, wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom; Irish nationalists, mostly Catholic, wanted a united Ireland. From 1968 a civil rights campaign modelled on the American one protested against discrimination in housing, employment and local electoral boundaries. It was met with violence, and the disorder after the Apprentice Boys parade in Derry on 12 August 1969 (the Battle of the Bogside) spread to Belfast, where streets were burned and thousands of families driven from their homes.

The Provisional IRA emerged from the split in Irish republicanism that followed and fought a campaign of shootings and bombings against the security forces, in Northern Ireland and in Britain; loyalist paramilitaries killed mostly Catholic civilians. Internment without trial from 1971 and the killing of thirteen unarmed marchers by paratroopers in Derry on Bloody Sunday in 1972 drove recruitment; direct rule from London followed.

Ceasefires in the 1990s led to [the Good Friday Agreement](event:good-friday-agreement) of 1998, which set up power-sharing institutions and provided for decommissioning. Sectarian division in housing and schooling persists, and sporadic violence continues.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles).

name: Apollo 11 Moon landing
summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon on 20 July 1969 and walked on its surface, watched on television by an estimated 600 million people.
body:
Part of [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program). Apollo 11 made the first crewed landing on the Moon. The lunar module Eagle touched down in the Sea of Tranquillity at 20:17 UTC on 20 July 1969, and Neil Armstrong stepped onto the surface some six and a half hours later, followed by Buzz Aldrin; Michael Collins remained in orbit aboard the command module Columbia. An estimated 600 million people watched the broadcast, and the crew returned to Earth on 24 July.

The mission launched from Kennedy Space Center on 16 July on a Saturn V and reached lunar orbit three days later. The descent was not routine: the guidance computer raised alarms it had no room to handle, the autopilot was heading for a field of boulders, and Armstrong flew the last stretch manually, landing with about thirty seconds of fuel margin. His first words on the surface, *That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind*, were heard live.

The two men spent about two and a half hours outside and 21 and a half hours on the Moon in total. They collected 21.5 kilograms of rock and soil, planted a flag, took a call from President Nixon, and left behind a seismometer, a laser reflector still used to measure the Earth–Moon distance, and a plaque reading "We came in peace for all mankind". Eagle's ascent stage lifted them back to Columbia, and the crew splashed down in the Pacific and spent three weeks in quarantine.

The landing met the goal Kennedy had set in 1961 and settled the [Space Race](event:space-race) in the American favour. Five further Apollo crews landed by 1972, and no one has been back since. The samples were used to develop the giant-impact explanation of the Moon's origin.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11).

name: ARPANET and the Internet
summary: The first packet-switched network linked four American universities; TCP/IP made networks of networks possible.
body:
ARPANET was the first large packet-switched computer network and the direct ancestor of the [Internet](item:global-internet). It was funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency of the American defence department, and its first link carried a message from the University of California, Los Angeles to the Stanford Research Institute on 29 October 1969. Four sites were connected by the end of that year.

Packet switching (breaking a message into pieces that find their own way and are reassembled at the far end) had been proposed independently by Paul Baran in the United States and Donald Davies in Britain. It used a shared network efficiently and had no central exchange to fail. The nodes were small computers called Interface Message Processors, which let machines of different makes join a common network.

Electronic mail appeared in 1971 and was soon most of the traffic. The problem that remained was joining separately administered networks to each other; the answer was the TCP/IP protocol suite designed by Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn, adopted across the network on 1 January 1983. That is the point at which an internet, a network of networks, existed.

ARPANET itself was shut down in 1990, by which time academic and commercial networks had taken over. The [World Wide Web](event:www), written that year, was built on top of it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET).

name: The Internet
summary: A network of networks joined by common protocols, in which no central authority routes traffic and any connected machine can address any other.
body:
The founding idea is packet switching: break a message into pieces, let each find its own way, reassemble at the far end. It is robust because there is no exchange to destroy and no circuit to hold open, and it was demonstrated on [ARPANET](item:internet) in 1969 between four American universities.

What made an internet rather than a network was TCP/IP, adopted in 1983, which let separately administered networks interconnect without agreeing on anything but the protocol. The design pushes intelligence to the endpoints and keeps the middle simple, which is why the [World Wide Web](item:www) could be added in 1990 without permission from anyone.

The machinery underneath is the [transistor](item:transistor), the [microprocessor](item:microprocessor) and the fibre-optic cable; the intellectual foundation runs back through [Turing's](item:alan-turing) definition of computation. Roughly two-thirds of humanity is now connected, mostly through devices in the tradition of the [smartphone](item:iphone), and the same properties that make the network difficult to censor make it difficult to police.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet).

name: Apollo 13
summary: An oxygen tank exploded on the way to the Moon; the crew improvised their way home in the lunar module.
body:
Part of [Apollo programme](event:apollo-program). Apollo 13 was to be the third Moon landing. Two days out, on 13 April 1970 and about 320,000 kilometres from Earth, an oxygen tank in the service module exploded, crippling the spacecraft's power, water and oxygen supplies. The landing was abandoned and the crew (James Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise) returned alive on 17 April.

The tank had been damaged before launch and its thermostat was wrong for the voltage used in testing; the insulation on its wiring burned when the tank was stirred, and the tank ruptured. The command module was left with only its re-entry batteries, so the crew moved into the lunar module and used it as a lifeboat, looping around the Moon to get home.

The lunar module was built to support two men for two days and had to keep three alive for four. Mission control worked out how to fit the command module's square carbon dioxide filters into the lander's round fittings with parts on board, and how to restart a frozen command module on almost no power. The crew splashed down in the Pacific in sight of the recovery ship.

Apollo flights stopped for ten months while the oxygen tanks were redesigned. NASA has often described the mission as a successful failure.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13).

name: The microprocessor
summary: Intel put a whole central processing unit on a single chip in 1971.
body:
Part of [Invention of the transistor](event:transistor). Intel announced the 4004 in November 1971: a whole central processing unit on one chip. It held about 2,300 transistors, worked on four bits at a time, and had been designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor and Masatoshi Shima for a Japanese calculator maker. Making the logic general and putting the specific behaviour in software was cheaper than designing custom chips for each product.

Others reached the same idea at about the same time (Texas Instruments' TMS 1000 and the classified processor of the F-14 fighter are the usual rival claims), but the 4004 and its successors made it an industry. The 8-bit 8080 of 1974 was the basis of the first personal computers, and the 8086 of 1978 started the x86 line that still dominates desktop and server machines.

The number of transistors on a chip has doubled roughly every two years for half a century, an observation made by Gordon Moore in 1965 and treated by the industry as a target. A processor today holds tens of billions of transistors and costs less in real terms than the 4004. Cheap general-purpose computation is what put computers in cars, telephones and appliances, and what made the [Internet](item:global-internet) and the [smartphone](event:iphone) possible.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprocessor).

name: Watergate scandal
summary: A burglary at Democratic Party headquarters in Washington unravelled into a scandal that forced Richard Nixon to resign, the only US president ever to do so.
body:
Watergate was an American political scandal that began with a burglary at the Democratic National Committee's offices in the Watergate complex in Washington on 17 June 1972 and ended with the resignation of President Richard Nixon on 9 August 1974. He is the only American president to have resigned the office.

The five men arrested were connected to Nixon's re-election committee, and the White House called the break-in a third-rate burglary. Reporting by the Washington Post, the trial judge's pressure on the defendants, and televised Senate hearings in 1973 traced it to a wider programme of political espionage, wiretapping and sabotage, funded from secret campaign money and covered up with hush payments and false testimony.

The decisive fact was that Nixon had recorded his own conversations. He fought the subpoenas for the tapes through the courts and dismissed the special prosecutor investigating him, in the Saturday Night Massacre of October 1973, which cost him much of his remaining support. In July 1974 the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released and the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment; a recording from six days after the burglary showed Nixon ordering the FBI inquiry obstructed. He resigned rather than face trial in the Senate, and his successor Gerald Ford pardoned him a month later.

Nearly fifty people were convicted, among them the attorney general and Nixon's closest aides. The scandal produced campaign finance limits, an independent counsel law, a stronger Freedom of Information Act and a durable public suspicion of the presidency; the suffix "-gate" has been attached to scandals ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal).

name: 1973 oil crisis
summary: Arab oil producers embargoed states supporting Israel in October 1973; the price of oil roughly quadrupled and the postwar boom in the West came to an end.
body:
The Organization of Arab Petroleum Exporting Countries announced an embargo in October 1973 against states it regarded as supporting Israel in the Yom Kippur War, and cut production. The posted price of crude oil rose from about three dollars a barrel to nearly twelve within a few months. The embargo was lifted in March 1974, but the price stayed high.

Western economies had been built around cheap oil, and consumption had risen every year since 1945. The immediate effects were petrol queues and rationing, speed limits, and bans on Sunday driving in several European countries. The wider effect was economic: the developed world entered a recession in which inflation and unemployment rose together, a combination the prevailing economic models did not expect and which was named stagflation.

It was also a demonstration that producer states, rather than the international oil companies, now set the terms. Members of OPEC had been nationalising their oil industries through the early 1970s, and the revenue transferred to them was very large.

The responses shaped energy policy for decades: fuel-economy standards for cars, strategic petroleum reserves, a rapid expansion of nuclear power in France and Japan, exploration in the North Sea and Alaska, and the first serious government interest in energy efficiency and renewable sources. A second shock followed the [Iranian revolution](event:iranian-revolution) in 1979.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis).

name: Soweto uprising
summary: School students in Soweto marched against compulsory teaching in Afrikaans; police opened fire, and the killings turned a protest into a national revolt against apartheid.
body:
School students in Soweto, the black township outside Johannesburg, marched on 16 June 1976 against a government order that half their lessons be taught in Afrikaans. Police opened fire on the march. The shootings set off months of protest across South Africa and turned a school dispute into a national revolt against apartheid.

Afrikaans was the language of the government that had built the apartheid system, and the decree was applied to schools that were already overcrowded, underfunded and staffed by teachers who did not speak it. Some 10,000 to 20,000 pupils joined the march. Among the first killed was 12-year-old Hector Pieterson; a photograph of his body being carried from the scene was published around the world.

Official figures put the dead at 176; other estimates run to several hundred, many of them children, over the weeks of unrest that followed. The United Nations Security Council condemned the killings, foreign investment slowed, and the sports and cultural boycotts of South Africa tightened.

Thousands of young people left the country to join the armed wings of the banned liberation movements, and the generation radicalised in 1976 sustained the resistance of the 1980s that ended in the negotiated [end of apartheid](event:apartheid-end). 16 June is a public holiday in South Africa.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_uprising).

name: Voyager probes launched
summary: Two spacecraft toured the outer planets and are now the most distant human-made objects, in interstellar space.
body:
NASA launched two spacecraft in 1977 to survey the outer planets: Voyager 2 on 20 August and Voyager 1 on 5 September, on a faster path that reached Jupiter and Saturn first. Both flew past Jupiter and Saturn; Voyager 2 went on to Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989 and remains the only spacecraft to have visited either.

The missions used a rare alignment of the outer planets, which occurs about every 175 years and allowed each planet's gravity to bend the craft towards the next. They returned the first close observations of the giant planets' atmospheres, ring systems, magnetic fields and moons: volcanic eruptions on Io, the possibility of an ocean under the ice of Europa, the nitrogen atmosphere of Titan, geysers on Triton.

Each carries a gold-plated copper record of sounds, music, greetings and images from Earth, assembled by a committee under Carl Sagan against the small chance that someone will one day find it. On its way out Voyager 1 turned its camera back in 1990 to photograph the planets from beyond Neptune, producing the image of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot.

Both have since crossed the heliopause into interstellar space (Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018) and both were still returning data into the 2020s, with instruments switched off one by one as their nuclear power sources decay. Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_program).

name: Camp David Accords
summary: Egypt and Israel agreed a framework for peace after thirteen days of talks at the US presidential retreat, leading to a treaty signed the following year.
body:
President Jimmy Carter brought Egypt's Anwar Sadat and Israel's Menachem Begin to the presidential retreat at Camp David in Maryland for thirteen days of talks in September 1978. The two signed a pair of frameworks on 17 September: one for a peace treaty between their countries, the other for Palestinian self-government in the West Bank and Gaza.

The talks followed Sadat's visit to Jerusalem in November 1977, the first by an Arab head of state, and the stalemate that had persisted since the [Six-Day War](event:six-day-war) of 1967 and the war of 1973. Carter kept the two delegations apart for much of the fortnight and carried proposals between them.

The Egypt–Israel peace treaty was signed in Washington on 26 March 1979. Israel withdrew from the Sinai peninsula in stages, completing the handover in 1982; Egypt recognised Israel, the first Arab state to do so; and the United States began the large annual military aid to both countries that continues. Sadat and Begin shared the Nobel Peace Prize for 1978.

The Palestinian half of the agreement was never implemented, and the Arab League suspended Egypt's membership and moved its headquarters out of Cairo for a decade. Sadat was assassinated by Islamist officers in 1981. The treaty itself has held for more than forty years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camp_David_Accords).

name: Iranian Revolution
summary: The shah was overthrown in 1979 and Iran became an Islamic republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.
body:
Mass strikes and street protests through 1978 forced Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, the shah of Iran, to leave the country on 16 January 1979. Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February and the imperial government collapsed within days. A referendum in March approved an Islamic republic, and a constitution adopted that year gave ultimate authority to a Shia cleric as supreme leader.

The shah had ruled with wide powers since a coup organised by British and American intelligence restored him in 1953. His land reform and industrial programme had produced rapid growth, inflation and a large displaced urban population; his secret police, SAVAK, suppressed opposition. Opposition came from clergy, bazaar merchants, communists and liberal nationalists alike; Khomeini's network of mosques and his sermons circulated on cassette tape gave it a common voice.

The revolutionary coalition did not survive its victory. Liberal and left-wing groups were removed from the new institutions within two years, and thousands of opponents were executed. Students seized the American embassy in November 1979 and held 52 diplomats for 444 days. Iraq invaded in 1980, beginning an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands.

The revolution turned Iran from an American ally into an adversary, encouraged Islamist movements across the region, and set off the Sunni–Shia rivalry with Saudi Arabia that runs through Middle Eastern politics. A second [oil shock](event:oil-crisis) followed in 1979.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_Revolution).

name: Three Mile Island nuclear accident
summary: A stuck valve and misread instruments led to a partial meltdown at a Pennsylvania reactor, the most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power.
body:
The most serious accident in the history of American commercial nuclear power took place at the Three Mile Island station near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, on 28 March 1979. A cooling malfunction in the Unit 2 reactor, made worse by a valve stuck open and instruments that misled the operators, uncovered the core and melted about half of it. The containment building held.

The plant lost feedwater to its steam generators; a relief valve opened and failed to shut, and the control room had no direct indication that it was still open. Operators, reading a high water level in the pressuriser, cut back the emergency cooling that would have saved the core. The sequence became the textbook case of an accident caused by the interface between machine and operator rather than by a single component.

Measured radiation doses to the surrounding population were small, and no deaths or illnesses have been reliably attributed to the release. Communication in the first days was confused, and an advisory to pregnant women and small children prompted some 140,000 people to leave the area.

The accident transformed the industry and its regulation: control rooms, training and emergency planning were overhauled, and public confidence in nuclear power in the United States collapsed. No new reactor ordered after 1978 was completed for three decades. [Chernobyl](event:chernobyl) followed seven years later, with far greater consequences. The damaged unit's cleanup took until 1993.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Mile_Island_accident).

name: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan
summary: Soviet troops invaded in December 1979 to support a communist government; they withdrew in 1989 after nine years of war.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Soviet forces entered Afghanistan in late December 1979, killed the communist president Hafizullah Amin and installed Babrak Karmal in his place. They stayed for nine years, fighting an insurgency they could not defeat, and completed their withdrawal on 15 February 1989.

The communist government that had taken power in 1978 had lost control of much of the countryside after attempting rapid land reform and secularisation. Moscow intervened to hold it up. The Soviet army held the cities, the airfields and the main roads; the mujahideen held the mountains and the villages, and were armed and financed by the United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with the shoulder-fired Stinger missiles supplied from 1986 blunting Soviet air power.

Around a million Afghans died, most of them civilians, and five million more fled to Pakistan and Iran in what was then the largest refugee movement in the world. Some 15,000 Soviet soldiers were killed. Mikhail Gorbachev called the war a bleeding wound and negotiated the withdrawal.

The defeat damaged the authority of the Soviet leadership two years before [the union dissolved](event:soviet-collapse). Afghanistan fell into civil war between the victorious factions; the Taliban took Kabul in 1996, and the networks formed among the foreign volunteers of the 1980s produced al-Qaeda and, eventually, [the American war](event:afghanistan-war) of 2001.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War).

name: Solidarity movement emerges in Poland
summary: Strikes in Gdańsk won the Soviet bloc's first independent trade union, led by Lech Wałęsa; banned under martial law in 1981, it won partly free elections in 1989.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). Strikes at the Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk in August 1980 forced Poland's communist government to accept an independent trade union, the first in the Soviet bloc. Solidarity, led by an electrician named Lech Wałęsa, was registered that November and claimed about ten million members within a year, a quarter of the country's population.

The strikes began over the sacking of a crane operator and rising food prices, and grew into a list of twenty-one demands that included the right to strike, the release of political prisoners and less censorship. The Gdańsk Agreement of 31 August 1980 conceded them. The movement drew on the Catholic Church, which had gained confidence from the election of the Polish pope John Paul II in 1978, and on intellectuals who had organised workers' defence committees after earlier protests were crushed.

General Wojciech Jaruzelski declared martial law on 13 December 1981, interned thousands of activists and banned the union, with Soviet intervention the alternative. Solidarity survived underground with support from the Church and from abroad; Wałęsa received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983.

By 1989 the economy was failing and the government opened round-table talks. Partly free elections on 4 June 1989 returned Solidarity candidates in almost every seat they could contest, and a non-communist prime minister took office in August, the first in the bloc, months before [the Berlin Wall opened](event:berlin-wall-fall). Wałęsa was elected president in 1990.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solidarity_(Polish_trade_union)).

name: Eradication of smallpox
summary: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980, the only human disease deliberately eliminated.
body:
The World Health Organization certified the eradication of smallpox on 8 May 1980. It is the only human disease to have been deliberately eliminated. The last naturally occurring case was diagnosed in a hospital cook in Somalia in October 1977; the last death was a medical photographer infected in a laboratory accident in Birmingham, England, in 1978.

Smallpox killed roughly three in ten of those it infected and scarred or blinded many who survived. It is estimated to have killed some 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. Eradication was possible because the virus has no animal reservoir, because infection is visible as a rash, and because [vaccination](event:smallpox-vaccine), the technique Edward Jenner published in 1798, gives durable protection.

The intensified WHO campaign began in 1967, when the disease was still endemic in 31 countries. Mass vaccination alone did not finish it; the method that did was surveillance and containment, in which every reported case was traced and everyone around it vaccinated, breaking the chains of transmission. The bifurcated needle made the injections quick and cheap enough to do at scale, and the last endemic reservoirs in India, Bangladesh, Ethiopia and Somalia were closed between 1975 and 1977.

Routine vaccination stopped after 1980. Known stocks of the virus remain in two secure laboratories, in the United States and Russia, and whether to destroy them is still argued. The campaign is the model for the effort against [polio](event:polio-vaccine).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox).

name: AIDS epidemic identified
summary: US doctors reported clusters of rare infections in previously healthy young men, the first recognition of the disease later named AIDS.
body:
American doctors reported clusters of rare infections in previously healthy young men in June 1981: pneumocystis pneumonia in Los Angeles and Kaposi's sarcoma in New York. It was the first recognition of the disease named acquired immune deficiency syndrome the following year. The virus that causes it, HIV, was isolated in 1983 at the Pasteur Institute.

HIV destroys the immune cells that defend against infection and is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, shared needles and from mother to child. It had been spreading unrecognised in central Africa for decades. Early cases in the United States and Europe were concentrated among gay men, injecting drug users and people with haemophilia, which shaped a public response marked by fear and stigma; activist groups such as ACT UP campaigned for faster drug approval and against neglect.

About 40 million people have died of AIDS-related illness, and a similar number live with HIV today, two-thirds of them in sub-Saharan Africa, where life expectancy in the worst-affected countries fell by more than a decade in the 1990s.

Combination antiretroviral therapy from 1996 turned the infection into a manageable chronic condition where the drugs were available; the argument over access, patents and generic manufacture that followed changed global health policy, and programmes such as PEPFAR and the Global Fund brought treatment to tens of millions. There is still no vaccine and no cure.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS).

name: Falkland Islands War
summary: Argentina invaded the British Falkland Islands; Britain retook them in a ten-week war fought thousands of miles from Europe.
body:
Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory in the South Atlantic, on 2 April 1982. Britain sent a naval task force 13,000 kilometres south and retook the islands after ten weeks of fighting; the Argentine garrison surrendered on 14 June. Some 649 Argentine and 255 British personnel died, along with three islanders.

Argentina had claimed the islands, which it calls the Malvinas, since Britain occupied them in 1833; the 1,800 inhabitants were and remain British. The military junta under General Leopoldo Galtieri, facing economic collapse and protests at home, expected a quick success and little British response. The United Nations Security Council demanded withdrawal, and Britain assembled a task force within days.

The fighting was mostly at sea and in the air. A British submarine sank the cruiser General Belgrano with 323 dead, the war's most disputed action, and Argentine aircraft with Exocet missiles sank several British ships, among them HMS Sheffield. Troops landed at San Carlos on 21 May and advanced across East Falkland to Port Stanley.

The junta fell within a year and Argentina returned to civilian government in 1983. In Britain the victory revived Margaret Thatcher's government, which won a large majority in 1983. The islands are now garrisoned; Argentina maintains its claim, which the islanders rejected in a referendum in 2013.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falklands_War).

name: Chernobyl disaster
summary: A reactor was destroyed during a safety test in April 1986; fallout spread across Europe and the area around the plant was permanently evacuated.
body:
Reactor number four at the Chernobyl nuclear power station in Soviet Ukraine was destroyed in the early hours of 26 April 1986 during a safety test. A power surge ruptured the fuel channels, two explosions blew the reactor apart and set its graphite moderator burning, and the fire carried radioactive material into the atmosphere for ten days. It is the worst nuclear accident in history.

The test was meant to show that the turbines could power the cooling pumps during a power cut. It was run at low power by a crew who had disabled safety systems and did not know that the RBMK design became unstable in exactly those conditions, or that inserting the control rods would briefly increase reactivity rather than reduce it. The reactor had no containment building of the kind Western designs use.

The fallout was heaviest in Ukraine, Belarus and western Russia, and was detected across Europe, first reported from a Swedish plant, which is how the accident became known outside the Soviet Union. The town of Pripyat was evacuated the next day; some 350,000 people were resettled in the end, and an exclusion zone of about 2,600 square kilometres remains. Two workers died in the explosion and 28 more of acute radiation sickness within months; thousands of thyroid cancers followed among those exposed as children, and estimates of total deaths from long-term exposure vary widely.

Hundreds of thousands of conscripts and workers, the liquidators, cleaned the site and built a concrete sarcophagus over the ruin; a steel arch was slid over that in 2016. The accident and the initial silence damaged Soviet credibility at home and abroad; Mikhail Gorbachev later wrote that the accident was a turning point for glasnost. Nuclear safety practice was revised worldwide.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernobyl_disaster).

name: Montreal Protocol
summary: Every country agreed to phase out CFCs to protect the ozone layer.
body:
The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer was signed on 16 September 1987 and came into force in 1989. It requires the phasing out of chlorofluorocarbons and related chemicals, and it is the only United Nations treaty ratified by every country in the world. It is generally described as the most successful environmental agreement yet made.

Chemists had proposed in 1974 that CFCs (stable, non-toxic gases used in refrigeration, aerosols and foam) would drift into the stratosphere and destroy ozone, which absorbs most of the sun's ultraviolet radiation. The discovery of a seasonal ozone hole over Antarctica, published by British Antarctic Survey scientists in 1985, turned a theoretical argument into an observed one, and the treaty followed two years later.

Its design was a phase-out timetable rather than a target, tightened repeatedly as the science improved, with money and later deadlines for developing countries and trade restrictions on non-parties. Substitutes were available and the affected industries eventually supported it.

Production of the controlled chemicals has fallen by about 99 per cent, atmospheric concentrations are declining, and the ozone layer is expected to return to its 1980 state around the middle of this century. Because CFCs are also powerful greenhouse gases, the treaty avoided a substantial amount of [warming](event:global-warming); the Kigali Amendment of 2016 extends it to their replacements for that reason.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal_Protocol).

name: Tiananmen Square protests
summary: Students and workers occupied the centre of Beijing for seven weeks demanding reform; the army cleared the square by force, killing hundreds or more.
body:
Students occupied Tiananmen Square in the centre of Beijing from April 1989, demanding an end to corruption, freedom of the press and political reform. The protests spread to hundreds of cities and drew in workers and ordinary residents. The army cleared central Beijing with tanks and live fire on the night of 3–4 June, killing hundreds and possibly several thousand people.

The occupation began with mourning for Hu Yaobang, a reformist party leader who died on 15 April; hunger strikes in May drew crowds of up to a million, embarrassing the leadership during a state visit by Mikhail Gorbachev. The Communist Party split over how to respond. Zhao Ziyang, who argued for negotiation, was removed and spent the rest of his life under house arrest; Deng Xiaoping and the hard-liners declared martial law on 20 May and brought in units from outside the capital.

Most of the killing took place on the approach roads west of the square rather than in it. Official figures give around 200 to 300 dead; estimates from other sources, including diplomatic cables, run into the thousands. Thousands were arrested afterwards, and a photograph of a man standing in front of a column of tanks on 5 June became one of the most reproduced images of the century.

Western governments imposed arms embargoes and suspended contacts, though most resumed trade within a few years. Economic liberalisation continued and political liberalisation stopped. Discussion of the events is censored in China, where they are absent from textbooks and from the internet.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre).

name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: East Germany opened its border on the evening of 9 November 1989 after a confused press conference; crowds crossed freely for the first time in 28 years.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). East Germany opened the [Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall) on the evening of 9 November 1989. A government spokesman, announcing new travel rules at a televised press conference and asked when they took effect, said immediately, without delay. Crowds gathered at the checkpoints within hours, the guards had no orders and no wish to shoot, and shortly before midnight the crossing at Bornholmer Straße was opened. The wall had stood for 28 years.

The pressure had been building all year. Hungary began dismantling its fence on the Austrian border in May and opened it in September, letting thousands of East German holidaymakers leave; others occupied West German embassies in Prague and Warsaw. Weekly demonstrations in Leipzig grew from hundreds to hundreds of thousands, and passed off without the crackdown many expected. Mikhail Gorbachev had made clear that Soviet troops would not be used to hold the East German government up, and Erich Honecker was removed by his own politburo in October.

The opening of the wall was not planned and the announcement was a misstatement of a decision that was to have taken effect the following day. Berliners crossed, drank and chipped at the concrete through the night; the first sections were removed by crane within days.

The communist governments of Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania fell within weeks. Germany was [reunified](event:german-reunification) less than a year later, and the [Soviet Union](event:soviet-collapse) dissolved in December 1991. The photographs of that night remain the standard image of the end of the Cold War in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Berlin_Wall).

name: World Wide Web
summary: Tim Berners-Lee proposed a hypertext system at CERN in 1989; released without charge, it became the way most people use the Internet.
body:
Part of [ARPANET and the Internet](event:internet). Tim Berners-Lee, a British software engineer at CERN, circulated a proposal for a hypertext information system in March 1989. He wrote the first server, the first browser and the first page in 1990, and the World Wide Web went outside the laboratory in 1991. It is the system of linked documents that most people mean when they say the internet.

The problem it solved was local: CERN's physicists used incompatible machines and lost track of each other's documents. The answer had three parts: a way to name any document anywhere (the URL), a way to ask a server for it (HTTP) and a way to write it with links to others (HTML), all built on top of the existing [Internet](event:internet). Hypertext had been described decades earlier; what was new was that a link could point at a document on any machine in the world, and that a broken link broke nothing else.

CERN put the specifications and the code in the public domain on 30 April 1993, without patent or royalty. That decision, and the free Mosaic browser released the same year, are usually credited with the Web's growth: a few dozen servers in 1992 became hundreds of thousands within three years.

Berners-Lee founded the World Wide Web Consortium in 1994 to keep the standards open. The Web carried commerce, publishing, and later [social networks](event:facebook-founded) and video, and it moved from desktop machines to [phones](event:iphone). Its openness also allowed the concentration that followed: a handful of companies now handle most of the traffic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web).

name: Reunification of Germany
summary: East and West Germany merged less than a year after the Berlin Wall fell, reuniting a nation divided for forty-five years.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Berlin Wall](event:berlin-wall-fall). East and West Germany were reunified on 3 October 1990, eleven months after the wall was opened. The German Democratic Republic acceded to the Federal Republic under the West German constitution, and a country divided since 1949 became one state of about 80 million people.

It happened quickly because the East German state was collapsing: its citizens were leaving, its economy was failing, and the first free elections in March 1990 returned a large majority for parties that wanted unity soon. A currency union on 1 July exchanged eastern marks for Deutsche Marks at rates generous to savers and ruinous for eastern industry.

The international obstacle was settled by the Two Plus Four Treaty of 12 September 1990, in which the two German states and the four wartime occupying powers agreed to full German sovereignty. Germany accepted the Oder–Neisse line as its eastern border permanently, limited the size of its armed forces, and renounced nuclear, biological and chemical weapons; Soviet troops were to leave by 1994. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government also gave assurances about European integration, and gave up the Deutsche Mark for the euro agreed at [Maastricht](event:maastricht).

Integration was expensive. Eastern factories closed, unemployment rose sharply, and transfers financed by a solidarity surcharge have run into the trillions of euros. Incomes and productivity in the east remain below western levels, and the political consequences of that gap are still argued over.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reunification).

name: Breakup of Yugoslavia
summary: Yugoslavia fragmented into separate states, and the wars that followed brought the worst violence in Europe since 1945.
body:
Yugoslavia, a federation of six republics, broke apart between 1991 and 1992, and the wars that followed were the worst violence in Europe since 1945. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991, Macedonia in September and Bosnia and Herzegovina in early 1992. Around 130,000 people died and some four million were displaced.

The federation had been held together by Josip Broz Tito, who died in 1980, by the Communist Party and by a rotating presidency. Economic crisis through the 1980s and the collapse of communism removed the remaining glue, and politicians in the republics, Slobodan Milošević in Serbia above all, mobilised national grievances. The problem was that the internal borders did not match where people lived: large Serb populations lived in Croatia and Bosnia.

Slovenia left after ten days of fighting. The war in Croatia ran from 1991 to 1995; the war in Bosnia from 1992 to 1995 was the worst, with the three-year siege of Sarajevo, the systematic expulsions given the name ethnic cleansing, camps, and the murder of about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica in July 1995, which international courts have ruled a genocide. NATO air strikes and the Dayton Agreement of December 1995 ended it.

Kosovo followed: a Serbian campaign against its Albanian majority brought NATO bombing in 1999 and a declaration of independence in 2008. The wars produced the first international war crimes tribunal since Nuremberg, which indicted 161 people including Milošević, and left seven states where one had been.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakup_of_Yugoslavia).

name: First Gulf War
summary: Iraq annexed Kuwait in 1990; a US-led coalition authorised by the UN drove its forces out in six weeks of air and ground warfare.
body:
Iraq invaded and annexed Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A coalition of 35 countries led by the United States and authorised by the United Nations Security Council drove the Iraqi army out in six weeks of fighting between 17 January and 28 February 1991. Kuwait's government was restored and Saddam Hussein stayed in power.

Iraq, heavily indebted after eight years of war with Iran, accused Kuwait of overproducing oil and drilling across the border. The invasion put a fifth of the world's oil reserves under Baghdad's control and threatened Saudi Arabia, and it came at a moment when the [Cold War](event:cold-war) was ending, so Moscow did not block the Security Council. Half a million American troops were assembled in Saudi Arabia under Operation Desert Shield.

Operation Desert Storm opened with a five-week air campaign against Iraqi forces, command centres and infrastructure, watched live on television, and ended with a ground offensive that took a hundred hours. Coalition dead numbered in the hundreds; Iraqi military deaths ran to tens of thousands. Retreating troops set fire to some 600 Kuwaiti oil wells, which burned for months, and fired Scud missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia.

The coalition stopped short of Baghdad. Uprisings by Shia and Kurds, encouraged from Washington, were crushed; no-fly zones, weapons inspections and sanctions blamed for large numbers of civilian deaths followed, and American forces remained in the Gulf. Saddam Hussein was removed by [the invasion of 2003](event:iraq-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War).

name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December 1991 into fifteen independent states, ending both the communist system and the Cold War.
body:
Part of [The Cold War](event:cold-war). The Soviet Union ceased to exist on 26 December 1991, when its own parliament acknowledged the dissolution of the state founded by the [October Revolution](event:october-revolution) of 1917. Fifteen republics became independent countries; Mikhail Gorbachev, the last Soviet leader, had resigned the day before, and the Russian flag replaced the red flag over the Kremlin.

Gorbachev had taken office in 1985 intending to save the system by reforming it. Glasnost opened the press and permitted criticism, including of the party's own past; perestroika loosened central planning without putting a working market in its place, and shortages worsened. Once it became clear that force would not be used, national movements in the Baltic republics, the Caucasus and Ukraine turned from cultural demands to independence, and the [Eastern European governments](event:berlin-wall-fall) fell in 1989 without Soviet intervention.

Hard-liners in the party, army and KGB detained Gorbachev at his holiday house on 19 August 1991 and declared a state of emergency. The coup collapsed in three days, in part because crowds in Moscow gathered around Boris Yeltsin, the elected president of the Russian republic, and the troops would not act. Real authority passed to the republics; the Communist Party was suspended, and on 8 December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus agreed that the union was at an end.

The successor states inherited a collapsing economy, and the 1990s in Russia brought hyperinflation, privatisation to a small group of owners and a sharp fall in life expectancy. Nuclear weapons in Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan were transferred to Russia. The end of the superpower rivalry left the United States without a rival for a decade, and the terms of the settlement, above all NATO's expansion and the status of the Russian-speaking populations left outside Russia, remain the substance of Russian grievance, and the background to [the war in Ukraine](event:ukraine-invasion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_the_Soviet_Union).

name: Maastricht Treaty and the European Union
summary: The European Communities became the European Union, with a common currency to follow in 1999.
body:
The Treaty on European Union was signed at Maastricht in the Netherlands on 7 February 1992 and came into force on 1 November 1993. It created the European Union, committed most of its members to a single currency, and extended cooperation from trade into foreign policy, justice and policing. The euro followed as an accounting currency in 1999 and as notes and coins in 2002.

The European Communities had been an economic project since the 1950s. Maastricht added two intergovernmental pillars beside them (a common foreign and security policy, and cooperation on justice and home affairs) and created citizenship of the Union, with the right to live and vote in any member state. Monetary union was governed by convergence criteria on deficits, debt and inflation, and by an independent European Central Bank.

The timing was set by the end of the Cold War: France and others wanted a [reunified Germany](event:german-reunification) bound tightly into European institutions, and Germany accepted the loss of the Deutsche Mark on terms modelled on the Bundesbank.

Ratification was contested. Danish voters rejected the treaty in June 1992 and accepted it a year later with opt-outs; the French referendum passed by one per cent; Britain negotiated exemptions from the currency and the social chapter and left the Union altogether after the [referendum of 2016](event:brexit-referendum). The single currency's design, one monetary policy without a common budget, was tested in the euro crisis after 2009.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty).

name: Rwandan genocide
summary: Members of Rwanda's Hutu majority killed some 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi, and Hutu who opposed them, in about a hundred days in 1994.
body:
Between April and July 1994 members of Rwanda's Hutu majority killed some 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi, along with Hutu who opposed them, in about a hundred days. It was carried out largely with machetes and clubs by army units, the Interahamwe militia, local officials and civilians.

The distinction between Hutu and Tutsi had been hardened into an administrative category by Belgian colonial rule, which issued identity cards recording it. Cycles of violence since independence had driven many Tutsi into exile, and their descendants formed the Rwandan Patriotic Front, which invaded from Uganda in 1990. A peace agreement in 1993 was resisted by an extremist faction in the government, whose radio station named targets and urged listeners to kill.

The killing began on 7 April, the day after the aircraft carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali; who fired is still disputed. The United Nations force in the country had a narrow mandate and was cut rather than reinforced after ten Belgian peacekeepers were murdered, and no government intervened while the killing was under way. A French deployment in June created a zone in the south-west through which many perpetrators escaped.

The genocide ended when the RPF took the country in July. Two million Hutu fled to Zaire, where the camps became the seed of wars in Congo that killed millions more. An international tribunal and local gacaca courts tried hundreds of thousands of cases, and the absence of intervention in 1994 is a standard case in later debate over humanitarian intervention.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwandan_genocide).

name: End of apartheid in South Africa
summary: South Africa held its first election with universal suffrage in April 1994 and Nelson Mandela became president, ending 46 years of legal white minority rule.
body:
South Africa's first election open to all races was held between 26 and 29 April 1994. The African National Congress won 62 per cent of the vote and [Nelson Mandela](item:nelson-mandela), released from prison four years earlier after 27 years, was inaugurated as president on 10 May. It ended the system of legalised racial separation called apartheid, imposed by the National Party after 1948.

Apartheid classified every person by race and used that classification to determine where they could live, work, study and travel. Black South Africans, three-quarters of the population, were assigned citizenship of nominally independent homelands, and millions were forcibly removed to them. Opposition was met with bannings, detention without trial, torture and killings: Sharpeville in 1960, [Soweto](event:soweto-uprising) in 1976 and the states of emergency of the 1980s.

By the late 1980s the government faced an ungovernable country, international sanctions, a sports and cultural boycott, disinvestment and an economy in decline, while the end of the [Cold War](event:cold-war) removed the argument that it was a bulwark against communism. F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and released Mandela in February 1990; four years of negotiation followed, alongside violence that killed thousands and nearly destroyed the process. Mandela and de Klerk shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.

The settlement kept property and pensions largely intact and set up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which heard testimony in public and offered amnesty in exchange for full disclosure. The civil war many expected did not happen. Political equality was achieved; South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries in the world by income.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid).

name: Dolly the sheep cloned
summary: Scottish scientists cloned an adult sheep using nuclear transfer, proving that the genome of an adult cell could be reprogrammed.
body:
Dolly the sheep was the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. She was born at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh on 5 July 1996 and announced to the world in February 1997. The team led by Ian Wilmut and Keith Campbell had taken the nucleus of a cell from an adult ewe's mammary gland and put it into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed.

The result mattered because biologists had generally assumed that specialisation was one-way: once a cell had become skin or muscle or mammary tissue, the unused parts of its genome were switched off for good. Dolly showed that an egg could reset an adult nucleus to the state of a fertilised embryo. It took 277 attempts to produce her, and the technique (somatic cell nuclear transfer) remained inefficient.

She lived at Roslin, produced six lambs, and was put down in February 2003 at the age of six with a lung infection common in sheep kept indoors; whether cloning shortened her life is unresolved. Her body is on display at the National Museum of Scotland.

The announcement set off immediate argument about human cloning, which many countries banned. In research, the demonstration that adult cells can be reprogrammed led to induced pluripotent stem cells in 2006, made without eggs or embryos, and to the regenerative medicine and disease-modelling work built on them. Cloning is now used commercially for livestock and pets.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolly_(sheep)).

name: Kyoto Protocol signed
summary: Industrialised nations accepted binding limits on greenhouse gas emissions, the first treaty to put numbers on climate commitments.
body:
The Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997 at a UN climate conference in Kyoto and came into force in February 2005. It was the first agreement to put binding numerical limits on greenhouse gas emissions: developed countries collectively undertook to cut theirs to about 5 per cent below 1990 levels by 2008–12.

It applied the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (the industrialised countries had produced most of the accumulated emissions, so they were to act first), and developing countries, including China and India, took on no targets. That asymmetry was the reason the United States, then the largest emitter, signed but never ratified; Canada withdrew in 2011 after missing its target.

The protocol introduced the market instruments that dominate climate policy since: emissions trading, joint implementation, and the Clean Development Mechanism, under which a rich country could count emissions avoided by a project in a poor one.

Most parties met their targets, helped by the collapse of heavy industry in the former Soviet bloc, but global emissions rose by about a third over the period as production moved to countries with no limits. The successor negotiated at Paris in 2015 replaced binding quotas with pledges each country sets for itself, which was the price of getting every large emitter inside the same agreement. Both are responses to [modern global warming](event:global-warming); see the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto_Protocol).

name: Good Friday Agreement
summary: Ireland and Britain signed an agreement ending 30 years of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland, establishing a power-sharing government.
body:
Part of the settlement of [the Troubles](event:troubles-begin). The Good Friday Agreement was reached in Belfast on 10 April 1998 between the British and Irish governments and most of Northern Ireland's political parties. It ended three decades of conflict in which about 3,500 people had been killed, and it remains the basis of the province's government.

Its central idea is that Northern Ireland's constitutional status is for its people to decide: it stays in the United Kingdom while a majority wishes, and Britain and Ireland undertake to accept a vote for unity if one comes. Ireland amended its constitution to drop the territorial claim. Everyone born there may hold British or Irish citizenship, or both.

The institutions are built around power-sharing: an assembly elected by proportional representation, an executive in which the two largest communities must both take part, north–south bodies with the Republic and an east–west council with Britain. The agreement also provided for the early release of paramilitary prisoners, the decommissioning of weapons, a new police service and a commission on policing.

Referendums approved it on both sides of the border in May 1998: 71 per cent in Northern Ireland and 94 per cent in the Republic. Implementation was slow: the IRA completed decommissioning only in 2005, and devolved government has been suspended several times, most recently between 2022 and 2024. Paramilitary violence has not entirely stopped, and [Brexit](event:brexit-referendum) reopened the question of the border the agreement had made invisible, but the peace has held.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday_Agreement).

name: War in Afghanistan begins
summary: A US-led coalition invaded Afghanistan in October 2001, removed the Taliban government and stayed for twenty years.
body:
Part of the response to [9/11](event:9-11). A United States-led coalition began bombing Afghanistan on 7 October 2001 after the Taliban government refused to hand over Osama bin Laden. Working with the Northern Alliance on the ground, it removed the Taliban from power within two months. The war that followed lasted twenty years, the longest in American history, and ended with the Taliban back in Kabul.

Bin Laden escaped from the mountains at Tora Bora in December 2001 and was killed in Pakistan in 2011. A new Afghan government was installed under the Bonn Agreement and a NATO-led force took over security, combining counter-insurgency with the building of an army, a state and a school system; American troop numbers peaked at about 100,000 in 2010–11. The Taliban regrouped in the south and east and in sanctuaries across the Pakistani border.

Estimates of the dead run to about 170,000 to 240,000, including some 46,000 Afghan civilians and about 2,400 American service members. Trillions of dollars were spent; corruption and the opium economy grew alongside real gains in schooling, health care and the position of women in the cities.

The United States agreed terms with the Taliban in Doha in February 2020 and withdrew in 2021 without the Afghan government at the table. The army it had built collapsed in days; Kabul fell on 15 August 2021 during a chaotic airlift from the airport. The Taliban restored their emirate and closed secondary education to girls.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%932021)).

name: September 11 attacks
summary: Al-Qaeda hijackers flew airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon on 11 September 2001, killing 2,977 people and setting off two decades of war.
body:
Nineteen members of al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger aircraft in the eastern United States on the morning of 11 September 2001. Two were flown into the towers of the World Trade Center in New York, which collapsed within two hours; a third struck the Pentagon outside Washington; the fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers who had learned of the other attacks by telephone tried to reach the cockpit. 2,977 people were killed, from more than 90 countries.

The attacks were planned by al-Qaeda under Osama bin Laden, then based in Afghanistan, and had been in preparation for years; most of the hijackers were Saudi nationals, and several had trained at American flight schools. Bin Laden's stated grievances were American troops in Saudi Arabia, support for Israel and sanctions on Iraq. It was the deadliest attack on American soil and the deadliest incident for firefighters and police in United States history; 412 emergency workers died at the World Trade Center.

NATO invoked its mutual-defence clause for the first time; a US-led coalition [invaded Afghanistan](event:afghanistan-war) within a month to remove the Taliban government that sheltered al-Qaeda; the [invasion of Iraq](event:iraq-war) followed in 2003 on separate and contested grounds. The USA PATRIOT Act, the Department of Homeland Security, detention without trial at Guantánamo Bay, airport screening as it is now practised, and a large expansion of electronic [surveillance](event:snowden-leaks) all date from these years.

Bin Laden was killed by American special forces in Pakistan in May 2011. A national commission reported in 2004 on the intelligence failures that preceded the attacks; rescue and clean-up workers at the site have since suffered high rates of respiratory illness and cancer. The rebuilt site opened in stages from 2011 around a memorial on the towers' footprints.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks).

name: Invasion of Iraq
summary: A US-led coalition invaded Iraq in 2003 on the claim that it held weapons of mass destruction; none were found, and the occupation was followed by insurgency and sectarian war.
body:
A coalition led by the United States and Britain invaded Iraq on 20 March 2003, stating that Saddam Hussein's government held weapons of mass destruction and had links to al-Qaeda. Baghdad fell in three weeks and the government collapsed. No such weapons were found, and no operational link to al-Qaeda was established.

The invasion was not authorised by a specific Security Council resolution and split the Western alliance, with France, Germany and Russia opposed; the demonstrations against it in February 2003 were among the largest coordinated protests ever held. Saddam Hussein was captured in December 2003 and executed by the new Iraqi government in 2006.

The occupation met armed resistance. The dissolution of the Iraqi army and the removal of Ba'ath Party members from public employment put hundreds of thousands of armed and trained men out of work; an insurgency grew through 2004, and the bombing of a Shia shrine in 2006 set off a sectarian civil war with death squads and mass displacement. Photographs of American abuse of prisoners at Abu Ghraib appeared in 2004. A troop surge and the turn of Sunni tribes against al-Qaeda in Iraq reduced the violence from 2007.

Documented civilian deaths number about 200,000, and survey-based estimates of total war deaths run far higher. American forces left in 2011. The Iraqi state that remained was sectarian and weak, and the Islamic State grew out of the insurgency to seize a third of the country in 2014. A British inquiry reported in 2016 that the case for war had been presented with unwarranted certainty.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq).

name: Human Genome Project completed
summary: After thirteen years, an essentially complete sequence of the three billion base pairs of human DNA was published and placed in the public domain.
body:
The Human Genome Project published an essentially complete sequence of the human genome in April 2003, thirteen years after it began. It read the order of about three billion base pairs of DNA and found that they contain roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes, far fewer than the 100,000 many biologists had expected.

The project was an international public consortium funded chiefly by the American National Institutes of Health and Britain's Wellcome Trust, with laboratories in six countries. From 1998 it was in a race with Celera Genomics, a private company under Craig Venter using a faster whole-genome shotgun method and intending to patent findings. The two announced a joint draft in June 2000 and published in early 2001.

The consortium's rule, agreed at Bermuda in 1996, was that every sequence be released publicly within twenty-four hours, which kept the human genome out of private ownership and set the norm for data sharing in biology.

The cost of sequencing a human genome has fallen from around a billion dollars to a few hundred. Genomics is now routine in cancer treatment, rare disease diagnosis, ancestry testing and epidemiology; it is how variants of the [COVID-19 virus](event:covid) were tracked. Gaps in repetitive regions left by the 2003 sequence were finally closed in 2022. See also [CRISPR](event:crispr).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Genome_Project).

name: Facebook founded
summary: Mark Zuckerberg launched a social network from a Harvard dormitory in 2004; it grew to billions of users and is the largest outside China.
body:
Mark Zuckerberg and four fellow students launched TheFacebook from a Harvard dormitory on 4 February 2004 as a directory of students at the university. It spread to other campuses, opened to anyone over thirteen in September 2006, and passed a billion monthly users in 2012. Its parent company, renamed Meta in 2021, now reports around three billion daily users across its services.

The site's innovations were the news feed, which turned a set of profile pages into a stream of updates, and the real-name policy, which made the network a map of actual social ties. Both made it valuable to advertisers, who can target that map precisely; advertising is almost all of the company's revenue. It bought Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014, purchases later examined by competition regulators.

Social networking became the dominant use of the consumer internet, and Facebook the largest of the networks outside China. It has been credited with a part in the [Arab Spring](event:arab-spring) and blamed for the spread of misinformation, for the harvesting of profile data by Cambridge Analytica in the 2016 American election, and for amplifying hate speech in Myanmar. Internal research leaked in 2021 described effects on adolescent mental health.

The company has since put money into virtual reality and artificial intelligence, and its share of younger users has fallen to competitors built around video.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook).

name: Hurricane Katrina
summary: A hurricane that had peaked at Category 5 over the Gulf came ashore as a Category 3 and breached the levees protecting New Orleans, flooding most of the city.
body:
Hurricane Katrina came ashore in south-east Louisiana on the morning of 29 August 2005 as a Category 3 storm, having reached Category 5 over the Gulf of Mexico. Its storm surge breached the levees and floodwalls protecting New Orleans in more than fifty places, and about 80 per cent of the city flooded, in places to the rooftops. Some 1,400 people died, most of them in Louisiana, and more than a million were displaced along the Gulf coast.

New Orleans lies largely below sea level between the Mississippi and Lake Pontchartrain, and its defences had been built by the Army Corps of Engineers over decades. Investigations afterwards found that they failed through design and construction faults rather than because the storm exceeded what they were supposed to withstand.

The relief effort became a national scandal. Tens of thousands sheltered without adequate water, food or sanitation in the Superdome and the convention centre; the Federal Emergency Management Agency was slow and its director unqualified; those without cars, disproportionately poor and black, had been unable to leave before the storm.

Damage was estimated at about $125 billion, the costliest in American history at the time. New Orleans lost about a third of its population, and the black population of the city has not returned to pre-storm levels. A $14 billion rebuilding of the flood defences followed, and the storm became a reference point in arguments about extreme weather under [modern global warming](event:global-warming) and about who bears the cost of it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina).

name: The smartphone era
summary: The iPhone put a networked computer with a camera in a pocket, and within a decade most of humanity carried one.
body:
Apple released the first iPhone on 29 June 2007, six months after Steve Jobs demonstrated it. It combined a mobile telephone, an iPod and internet access in one device controlled entirely by a multi-touch screen, with no keyboard and no stylus, running a version of the Macintosh operating system. Its design became the pattern for the smartphone.

Smartphones already existed (BlackBerry, Nokia's Symbian devices and Windows Mobile) but they were built around keyboards and menus and treated the mobile web as a cut-down version of the real one. The iPhone put a usable browser on a phone, and the App Store, opened in 2008, turned the device into a platform anyone could write for. Google's Android, announced in 2007 and licensed free to manufacturers, followed the same model and now runs on the large majority of the world's phones.

Within a decade most adults on Earth carried one. The device is used for maps, messaging, photography, payment and banking in countries with few banks, and industries including taxis, hotels, retail and news reorganised around it. For much of the world's population a smartphone is the only computer and the only connection to the [Internet](item:global-internet).

[Social networks](event:facebook-founded) reached their scale on phones, and the effects of constant connection on sleep, attention and adolescent mental health are the subject of continuing research and dispute.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IPhone_(1st_generation)).

name: Barack Obama elected president
summary: Obama became the first African-American US president, amid the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.
body:
Barack Obama was elected president of the United States on 4 November 2008, defeating John McCain, and was inaugurated on 20 January 2009. He was the first African-American to hold the office, 45 years after the [March on Washington](event:march-washington) and 143 years after the abolition of slavery.

A first-term senator from Illinois and formerly a community organiser and constitutional law lecturer in Chicago, he won the Democratic nomination against Hillary Clinton after a long primary campaign notable for its use of small online donations and volunteer organising. The election was held six weeks after the collapse of Lehman Brothers, in the middle of the [financial crisis](event:financial-crisis), which dominated his first year in office.

His administration passed a large stimulus, rescued the car industry, and enacted the Affordable Care Act of 2010, which extended health insurance to some twenty million people and survived repeated challenges in the courts and Congress. Abroad he wound down the war in Iraq, ordered the raid that killed Osama bin Laden, negotiated the nuclear agreement with Iran and the [Paris Agreement](event:paris-agreement) on climate, and restored relations with Cuba. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in his first year, a decision widely criticised as premature.

He was re-elected in 2012. Congressional opposition hardened through both terms, much of the foreign policy was reversed by his successor, and the hope that his election marked a post-racial turn in American politics was not borne out.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama).

name: Global financial crisis
summary: The collapse of the American mortgage market brought down banks worldwide and caused the deepest recession since the 1930s.
body:
The global financial crisis of 2007–09 was the most severe economic downturn since the Great Depression. It began with rising defaults in the American subprime mortgage market, spread through the banks and funds that held mortgage-backed securities, and became a general freeze in credit after the investment bank Lehman Brothers failed on 15 September 2008.

A decade of rising house prices, low interest rates and light regulation had produced mortgages lent without checks, packaged into securities, rated far more safely than they deserved, and insured through derivatives that concentrated the risk rather than spreading it. Banks were highly leveraged and funded themselves from day to day, so when the value of the collateral became uncertain they could not borrow at all.

Governments and central banks responded with bank rescues, guarantees, near-zero interest rates and, later, large-scale purchases of assets (quantitative easing) together with fiscal stimulus coordinated through the G20. World trade and output fell sharply in 2009; unemployment rose into double figures in several countries, and about nine million American households lost their homes.

The aftermath ran for a decade: a sovereign debt crisis in the euro area from 2010, austerity programmes across Europe, a long argument about inequality and about whether the banks had been rescued and their borrowers abandoned, and new capital rules under Basel III. Its political effects are usually held to include Occupy, the Tea Party and the rise of parties outside the postwar mainstream.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007–2008_financial_crisis).

name: Arab Spring
summary: Protests spread from Tunisia across the Arab world, toppling four governments and setting off civil wars in Syria, Libya and Yemen.
body:
The Arab Spring was a wave of protests and uprisings across the Arab world in 2010–12. It began in Tunisia in December 2010 after a street vendor, Mohamed Bouazizi, set himself on fire when officials confiscated his cart, and spread within weeks to Egypt, Libya, Yemen, Bahrain, Syria and beyond. Four long-established rulers were removed; several countries fell into civil war.

The grievances were common to the region: unemployment among a young and educated population, rising food prices, police brutality, corruption and rulers who had held power for decades. Satellite television and social media carried events from one country to the next quickly, though how much they caused rather than transmitted the protests is argued over.

Tunisia's president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali fled in January 2011 and Egypt's Hosni Mubarak resigned in February after eighteen days of occupation of Tahrir Square in Cairo. In Libya an armed uprising, backed by a NATO air campaign, ended with Muammar Gaddafi's death in October. Yemen's president stepped down early in 2012. Bahrain's protests were put down with Saudi help.

The outcomes were mostly not democratic. Syria's crackdown became a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced half the country's population; its government fell only in December 2024. Libya and Yemen fragmented. Egypt elected an Islamist president in 2012 and returned to military rule in 2013. Tunisia, the one democratic transition, saw its president dismantle those institutions after 2021.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Spring).

name: Fukushima nuclear disaster
summary: An earthquake and tsunami knocked out cooling at a Japanese nuclear plant, and three reactor cores melted down in the worst nuclear accident since Chernobyl.
body:
The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant on Japan's Pacific coast lost its power supply when the tsunami of 11 March 2011 overtopped its sea wall. Without cooling, three reactor cores melted down over the following days, hydrogen explosions destroyed the buildings around them, and radioactive material was released to the air and sea. It is rated with [Chernobyl](event:chernobyl) at the top of the international scale of nuclear accidents.

The earthquake that caused the tsunami, magnitude 9.0 off Tōhoku, was the largest ever recorded in Japan. The reactors shut down automatically as designed; what failed was the backup cooling, whose diesel generators stood at ground level and were flooded. The plant's operator and the regulator had assessed the risk of a wave that size as negligible, a judgement a parliamentary inquiry later called a man-made failure of regulation rather than a natural disaster.

The tsunami itself killed about 18,000 people along the coast. The meltdowns caused no immediate radiation deaths; one worker's later cancer has been officially attributed to exposure. Some 150,000 people were evacuated, and more than 2,000 deaths have been attributed to the strain of displacement. Decommissioning is expected to take decades, and treated water stored on the site began to be released to the ocean in 2023 over protests from neighbouring states and local fishermen.

Japan shut down its entire reactor fleet for a time and has restarted only part of it; Germany brought forward a complete nuclear phase-out, completed in 2023. The accident set back low-carbon generation at a point when emissions needed to fall.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukushima_nuclear_accident).

name: Curiosity rover lands on Mars
summary: A one-tonne rover landed in Gale Crater in August 2012 to study whether Mars was once habitable.
body:
NASA's Curiosity rover landed in Gale Crater on Mars on 6 August 2012. About the size of a small car and weighing 899 kilograms, it was too heavy for the airbags used by earlier rovers and was lowered to the surface on cables from a rocket-powered descent stage (the sky crane) in a sequence that had never been tested end to end.

It launched from Cape Canaveral in November 2011 and is powered by a radioisotope generator rather than solar panels, so it works through dust storms and winter. Its instruments include a laser that vaporises rock at a distance to read its composition, a drill, and a small chemistry laboratory inside the body of the rover.

Its mission was to establish whether Mars ever offered conditions in which life could have existed. Within a year it had found rounded pebbles laid down by flowing water and mudstone from an ancient lakebed with the chemistry a microbe would need. It has since measured organic molecules in the rock, seasonal variations in atmospheric methane that are still unexplained, and radiation levels along the route a human crew would follow.

Designed for two years, it has worked for more than a decade, climbing the layered slopes of Mount Sharp in the middle of the crater. Its landing system was reused for the Perseverance rover in 2021.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity_(rover)).

name: Discovery of the Higgs boson
