summary: The LHC at CERN found the particle that completes the Standard Model and explains how other particles acquire mass.
body:
CERN announced on 4 July 2012 that two experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, ATLAS and CMS, had independently found a new particle with a mass of about 125 GeV that behaved like the Higgs boson. It was the last particle predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics that had not been observed.

The boson is the visible sign of the Higgs field, proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert, Robert Brout and others to explain why the carriers of the weak nuclear force are heavy while the photon is massless. In the theory the field fills all space, and particles acquire mass through their interaction with it. Without that mechanism the Standard Model predicts a universe with no atoms.

Finding it took the largest machine ever built: a 27-kilometre ring under the Swiss–French border in which protons collide 40 million times a second, and detectors the size of buildings recording the debris. The boson decays almost immediately, so it was identified statistically, as a small excess of particular decay products above the expected background.

Higgs and Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2013; Brout had died in 2011. The discovery completed the Standard Model without explaining what lies beyond it. Dark matter, the mass of neutrinos and the imbalance between matter and antimatter are all still outside the theory, and measuring the boson's properties precisely is one way of looking for what is missing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higgs_boson).

name: CRISPR gene editing
summary: A bacterial defence system was turned into a cheap and precise way of editing the DNA of any organism.
body:
CRISPR–Cas9 is a technique for editing genomes, published by Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier in 2012 and demonstrated in human cells the following year. A guide made of RNA carries a cutting enzyme to a chosen sequence of DNA, where it makes a break that the cell then repairs, disabling a gene or replacing it with a supplied version.

The parts were found in bacteria, which keep fragments of the viruses that have attacked them in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and use them to recognise and cut the same virus again. Earlier editing methods existed but required a new protein to be engineered for each target; CRISPR needs only a new strand of RNA, which is why it made gene editing cheap enough for ordinary laboratories.

Doudna and Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. The first approved CRISPR therapy, Casgevy, was licensed in Britain in November 2023 and in the United States in December for sickle-cell disease and beta thalassemia; it edits a patient's own blood stem cells outside the body. Trials are under way for other inherited conditions, and the technique is widely used in agriculture and in research on [genomes](event:human-genome) and [DNA](event:dna-structure).

Editing that can be inherited is another matter. A Chinese researcher who edited embryos that became children in 2018 was condemned internationally and imprisoned, and germline editing in humans is banned or unapproved almost everywhere.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRISPR_gene_editing).

name: Deep learning and modern AI
summary: Neural networks trained on large datasets became the basis of most modern artificial intelligence after 2012.
body:
Deep learning is machine learning with neural networks of many layers, trained on large quantities of data. The approach is old (the mathematics dates to the 1980s) but it became practical around 2012, when graphics processors made training fast enough and image collections made it possible to train on millions of examples.

The result that changed opinion was AlexNet, a network from Geoffrey Hinton's group at Toronto that won the ImageNet image-recognition contest in 2012 by a wide margin. Speech recognition and machine translation followed within a few years, and in 2016 a system built by DeepMind beat one of the strongest human players at Go, a game long thought out of reach.

The second turn came from a 2017 architecture called the transformer, designed for translation, which learns which parts of a sequence to attend to and trains efficiently on very large amounts of text. Scaling it up produced the large language models behind systems such as [ChatGPT](event:chatgpt-released), and the same methods produced AlphaFold's prediction of protein structures, image and video generation, and forecasting models used in weather and medicine. Hinton and John Hopfield shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024, and the AlphaFold team the prize in Chemistry.

Disputes about the technology continue: the electricity and capital required, the use of copyrighted material in training, systems that state falsehoods fluently, the effect on skilled work, and the governance of models whose capabilities are not fully understood by the people who build them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_learning).

name: Edward Snowden reveals NSA mass surveillance
summary: A former NSA contractor, speaking from Hong Kong, gave journalists documents showing that US and allied agencies collected phone and internet records on a mass scale.
body:
Edward Snowden, a contractor working for the American National Security Agency, gave journalists a large archive of classified documents in June 2013. The first stories, published in the Guardian and the Washington Post from 5 June, described the bulk collection of American telephone records and a programme of access to the data held by large internet companies.

Later disclosures described the tapping of undersea fibre-optic cables, the collection of hundreds of millions of contact lists, efforts to weaken encryption standards, surveillance of allied heads of government, and the sharing arrangements between the intelligence agencies of the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Snowden gave interviews from Hong Kong, was charged under the Espionage Act, and was stranded in Moscow when his passport was cancelled; he was granted Russian citizenship in 2022.

The disclosures set off a public argument about the scale of state surveillance. An American court found the telephone metadata programme unlawful, and Congress ended it in the USA Freedom Act of 2015; European courts struck down data transfer arrangements and a data retention directive.

One effect was technical. Encryption became standard: most web traffic is now encrypted in transit, and messaging services adopted end-to-end encryption by default, which in turn produced the continuing dispute between technology companies and governments over lawful access. Whether Snowden is a whistleblower or a criminal remains contested.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden).

name: Same-sex marriage legalized in the US
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry, following decades of activism and court battles.
body:
The United States Supreme Court ruled on 26 June 2015, in Obergefell v. Hodges, that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry. The decision, carried by five votes to four, required every state to license such marriages and to recognise those performed elsewhere, settling a question that had been fought state by state for a decade.

The case was brought by Jim Obergefell, who had married his dying partner on an aircraft on a runway in Maryland and wanted to be recorded as his spouse on the Ohio death certificate. The majority opinion, written by Justice Anthony Kennedy, held that the right to marry is fundamental under the due process and equal protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment; the dissenters argued that the question belonged to the states and to legislatures.

Massachusetts had been the first state to allow same-sex marriage, in 2004; by 2015 thirty-six states did. Public opinion had shifted faster than on almost any other American social question, from about a third in favour in the mid-2000s to a clear majority. Congress added a statutory guarantee of federal recognition in the Respect for Marriage Act of 2022, after a Supreme Court opinion questioned the reasoning behind such rights.

The ruling came 46 years after [the Stonewall uprising](event:stonewall-uprising). More than thirty countries now allow same-sex marriage, while consensual same-sex relations remain criminal in some sixty others.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obergefell_v._Hodges).

name: First detection of gravitational waves
summary: LIGO recorded ripples in spacetime from two merging black holes in September 2015, a century after Einstein predicted them.
body:
The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory recorded the collision of two black holes about 1.3 billion light-years away on 14 September 2015, the first direct detection of gravitational waves. The discovery was announced on 11 February 2016. [Einstein](event:relativity) had predicted such waves in 1916 and doubted they would ever be measurable.

A gravitational wave stretches and squeezes space as it passes. LIGO measures that by splitting a laser beam down two four-kilometre arms at right angles and recombining it; the passing wave changed the relative lengths by about a thousandth of the width of a proton. Two detectors, in Louisiana and Washington state, saw the same signal seven milliseconds apart, which is how a real event is told from local noise.

The signal lasted a fifth of a second and matched the predicted waveform of two black holes of about 29 and 36 solar masses spiralling together, and the first direct evidence that black holes of that size exist and merge. Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2017 for the decades of instrument work behind it.

Gravitational waves are a new way of observing: they come from events that emit little or no light. The merger of two neutron stars in 2017, seen by LIGO, Virgo and telescopes across the spectrum at once, showed where heavy elements such as gold are made. More than two hundred mergers have been recorded since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_observation_of_gravitational_waves).

name: Paris Agreement on climate change
summary: Nearly every country agreed to limit warming to well below 2 °C, with national pledges rather than binding quotas.
body:
The Paris Agreement was adopted at the twenty-first United Nations climate conference on 12 December 2015 and came into force on 4 November 2016. Its parties (194 states and the European Union) undertake to hold the rise in global average temperature well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

It works differently from the [Kyoto Protocol](event:kyoto-protocol), which set binding quotas on rich countries alone and which the United States never ratified. Under Paris every country sets its own target, a nationally determined contribution, and is expected to submit a stronger one every five years; progress is assessed collectively in a global stocktake, the first of which reported in 2023. The obligations of process are binding, the targets themselves are not. That design is what brought China, India and the United States inside the same agreement.

The pledges made do not add up to the goal. Global emissions have continued to rise, 2024 was the first calendar year to average more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial temperatures, and current policies point to considerably more warming than 2 °C by 2100. The agreement's provisions on finance for adaptation and for the losses of poorer countries have consistently fallen short of what was promised.

The United States withdrew in 2020, rejoined in 2021 and withdrew again with effect from January 2026. The agreement is the main international framework for the response to [modern global warming](event:global-warming).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Agreement).

name: Brexit referendum
summary: British voters chose to leave the European Union by 51.9 to 48.1 per cent; withdrawal took nearly four years.
body:
The United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union in a referendum on 23 June 2016. Leave took 51.9 per cent of the vote to Remain's 48.1, on a turnout of 72 per cent. David Cameron, who had called the referendum and campaigned to stay, resigned the next morning.

Britain had joined the European Communities in 1973 and voted to stay in a referendum two years later, but membership was never settled in British politics; the country stayed out of the single currency and the passport-free travel area agreed at [Maastricht](event:maastricht). The vote divided sharply by age, education and place: large majorities to leave in post-industrial England and Wales, majorities to remain in London, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Sovereignty and immigration were the leading arguments on one side, economic risk on the other.

Withdrawal took nearly four years, two prime ministers and two general elections. The hardest problem was Ireland: leaving the customs union and single market implied a border somewhere, and the [Good Friday Agreement](event:good-friday-agreement) depended on there being none on the island. The eventual answer placed the customs boundary in the Irish Sea, revised in 2023.

The United Kingdom left on 31 January 2020 and the transition period ended that December, with a trade agreement covering goods but little of the services that dominate the British economy. Official estimates put the long-run cost at a few per cent of national income; freedom of movement ended, though total immigration rose. Scotland's independence question and the European Union's own cohesion were both affected.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit).

name: MeToo movement emerges
summary: Accounts of sexual harassment and assault shared under the MeToo hashtag from October 2017 led to dismissals, prosecutions and changes in the law.
body:
MeToo is a movement against sexual harassment and assault that spread worldwide in October 2017. The phrase had been used since 2006 by the American activist Tarana Burke in work with survivors of sexual violence; it became a hashtag when the actress Alyssa Milano asked women who had been harassed or assaulted to reply with it, days after allegations against the film producer Harvey Weinstein were published.

The phrase was used hundreds of thousands of times within a day and appeared in millions of posts within a week, in dozens of languages, and accounts that had been treated as isolated incidents were widely discussed as a pattern. Investigations by the New York Times and the New Yorker into Weinstein, which shared a Pulitzer Prize, described decades of allegations kept quiet by settlements and non-disclosure agreements.

Hundreds of men in film, music, media, politics, business, sport and religion lost their positions in the following two years. Weinstein was convicted of sexual assault in New York in 2020 and in Los Angeles in 2022; the New York verdict was overturned on appeal in 2024 and the case was tried again. Legislatures in several countries limited non-disclosure agreements, extended time limits for prosecution and tightened workplace rules.

The movement drew criticism for accusations made without due process, for punishments that did not distinguish between very different acts, and for concentrating on wealthy industries while low-paid workers, who have least protection, were largely absent from the coverage.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Me_Too_movement).

name: COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A new coronavirus spread worldwide in early 2020, killing at least seven million people by confirmed count and many more by excess-death estimates, and shutting down much of ordinary life for two years.
body:
The COVID-19 pandemic was caused by SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus first identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. The World Health Organization declared a public health emergency on 30 January 2020 and called it a pandemic on 11 March; the emergency was ended on 5 May 2023. About 7 million deaths were confirmed, and estimates that count deaths above the normal rate put the true toll several times higher.

The virus spreads through the air, and a substantial share of transmission comes from people with no symptoms, which made containment difficult. Governments responded with border closures, school and business closures and stay-at-home orders of a kind not previously attempted at this scale; roughly half the world's population was under some form of restriction in April 2020. Health systems in many countries were overwhelmed in successive waves.

The scientific response was unusually fast. The genome was published in January 2020, and vaccines using messenger RNA (a technology developed over the previous three decades) were authorised within a year and given to billions of people. Distribution was very unequal between rich and poor countries. Treatments, oxygen supply and knowledge of the disease improved through the pandemic, and successive variants changed both its transmissibility and its severity.

The economic and social effects were large: the deepest global recession since the war, trillions spent on support programmes, a lasting shift to remote work, interrupted schooling, and an inflation surge that followed the reopening. The origin of the virus (spillover from animals at a market, or a laboratory accident) remains disputed, and the pandemic left political arguments about the balance between restriction and liberty in many countries. Comparisons were drawn throughout with the [1918 influenza pandemic](event:spanish-flu). Its phases are the steps of this saga.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic).

steps.name: The outbreak (January 2020)
steps.page: A cluster of pneumonia of unknown cause was reported in Wuhan at the end of December 2019, and the genome of the new coronavirus was published on 11 January 2020. China locked down Wuhan and the surrounding province on 23 January, confining some 50 million people; the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern on 30 January. Cases followed in Thailand, Italy, Iran and elsewhere, and by late February the outbreak was clearly no longer containable.

steps.name: Pandemic and lockdowns (March 2020)
steps.page: The WHO called the outbreak a pandemic on 11 March 2020. Within a fortnight Italy, Spain, France, India, Britain and much of the Americas had ordered people to stay at home, closed schools and shut all but essential business. Air travel almost stopped, borders closed, and hospitals in Lombardy, Madrid and New York ran out of intensive care beds. Stock markets fell sharply and governments announced support programmes on a very large scale.

steps.name: The first vaccines (December 2020)
steps.page: The first vaccinations outside clinical trials were given in Britain on 8 December 2020, less than a year after the virus was sequenced, far faster than any previous vaccine. Two of the leading products used messenger RNA, a method that had never before been licensed; others used viral vectors or inactivated virus. Supply went first to wealthy countries, and the COVAX scheme intended to share doses fell well short of its targets.

steps.name: The Delta wave (2021)
steps.page: The Delta variant, first identified in India, spread through 2021 and was substantially more transmissible than earlier forms. India's second wave in April and May overwhelmed hospitals and crematoria; many countries reimposed restrictions. Vaccination sharply reduced hospitalisation and death but did not stop transmission, and the year's argument turned to boosters, vaccine mandates and passports.

steps.name: Omicron (from November 2021)
steps.page: Omicron was reported by South African scientists on 24 November 2021 and spread faster than any previous variant, infecting many people who had been vaccinated or previously infected. It proved less likely to cause severe disease, and in most countries the combination of high immunity and lower severity was the point at which restrictions were dismantled. China held to elimination through repeated lockdowns until December 2022, then abandoned the policy in a matter of weeks.

steps.name: The end of the emergency (May 2023)
steps.page: The World Health Organization ended the public health emergency on 5 May 2023, saying the disease was now an established and continuing health problem rather than an emergency. SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and to evolve, with vaccines updated for the current variants. Long COVID (symptoms persisting for months after infection) affects a substantial minority of those infected and is still poorly understood.

name: James Webb Space Telescope
summary: A 6.5-metre infrared telescope launched to a point 1.5 million km from Earth to observe the first galaxies.
body:
The James Webb Space Telescope was launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana and reached its station near the Sun–Earth Lagrange point 2, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth, a month later. Built by NASA with the European and Canadian space agencies over some twenty-five years and about $10 billion, it is the largest telescope ever put in space.

Its primary mirror is 6.5 metres across, made of eighteen gold-coated beryllium segments that were folded for launch and unfolded in orbit, along with a sunshield the size of a tennis court that keeps the instruments near 40 kelvin. Nothing about that sequence could be tested end to end beforehand or repaired afterwards. It observes in the infrared, which is what lets it see the light of the earliest galaxies, stretched by the expansion of the universe, and through the dust that hides star formation.

The first images were released in July 2022. It has since found galaxies that formed within a few hundred million years of the Big Bang and appear brighter and more mature than models predicted, measured the chemistry of the atmospheres of planets around other stars, and photographed star-forming regions, planetary nebulae and the outer planets in new detail.

It succeeded Hubble as the principal space observatory for deep observation, though the two work at different wavelengths and both are in use. Its fuel and cold reserves are expected to allow operations for two decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope).

name: ChatGPT released
summary: OpenAI released a conversational interface to a large language model; it reached a hundred million users within two months and made generative AI a mass technology.
body:
OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022 as a free research preview: a chat window in front of a large language model. It reached a million users in five days and about a hundred million within two months, the fastest adoption of a consumer application recorded to that point, and it made generative artificial intelligence a mass technology.

The underlying models are transformers trained to predict the next fragment of text over very large quantities of writing, then tuned with human feedback to follow instructions and refuse some requests. Nothing in that was new. The [methods](event:deep-learning) had been developed over the previous decade, and OpenAI's own GPT-3 was two years old. What was new was the interface: anyone could type a question in ordinary language and get an answer that read as though a person had written it.

Uses spread quickly through writing, translation, summarising, tutoring and programming, and later versions added images, voice, web search and the ability to carry out multi-step tasks. Competitors followed within months from Google, Anthropic, Meta and Chinese laboratories, and the capital and electricity going into the data centres behind them became a substantial part of the economy. By early 2026 OpenAI reported hundreds of millions of weekly users.

The arguments about it include models that state falsehoods confidently, training on copyrighted work without permission, effects on schools, on entry-level professional work and on the market for online writing, and how systems of increasing capability should be governed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT).

name: Russian invasion of Ukraine
summary: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 in the largest war in Europe since 1945; about six million people have left the country.
body:
Russia invaded Ukraine on 24 February 2022 with missile strikes and ground advances on Kyiv, Kharkiv, the south and the Donbas. It is the largest war in Europe since 1945. The attempt on Kyiv failed within weeks, and the war became a long fight of artillery, drones and fortified lines across the east and south of the country.

It followed eight years of a smaller war: Russia annexed Crimea in 2014 after Ukraine's pro-Western revolution and backed separatist statelets in the Donbas. President Putin's stated reasons in 2022 were NATO enlargement and the claim that Ukraine is not a separate nation.

Ukrainian counteroffensives recovered Kharkiv province in September 2022 and Kherson city in November. A much-anticipated offensive in 2023 achieved little against dense minefields, and from 2024 Russian forces advanced slowly at heavy cost, taking Avdiivka, Pokrovsk and other towns in the Donbas; Ukraine held part of Russia's Kursk region for a time in 2024–25. Casualties on both sides run to hundreds of thousands killed and wounded; tens of thousands of Ukrainian civilians have been killed, cities such as Mariupol and Bakhmut destroyed, and about six million people have left the country with several million more displaced inside it.

European security arrangements changed with the war. Finland and Sweden joined [NATO](event:nato-founded), European states raised defence spending and cut their dependence on Russian gas, and Western governments supplied Ukraine with weapons and money while imposing extensive sanctions on Russia. Repeated negotiations have not produced a ceasefire, and the fighting continues.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine).

name: World population reaches 8 billion
summary: The UN marked an eightfold increase in human numbers since 1800, with growth now slowing worldwide.
body:
The United Nations marked 15 November 2022 as the day the world's population reached eight billion. The date is a projection rather than a count, and it records a rise from about one billion in 1800 and two and a half billion in 1950; most of the growth in human numbers has happened within a single lifetime.

The increase came from falling death rates rather than rising birth rates: vaccination, antibiotics, clean water, and the fertiliser and crop breeding of the [Green Revolution](event:green-revolution). Birth rates then fell too, everywhere they have been measured, as child mortality fell and women's education and employment spread, a process known as the demographic transition. Annual growth peaked at about 2.1 per cent in the late 1960s and is now below 1 per cent.

The distribution has shifted with it. India passed China as the most populous country in 2023; more than half of the growth to 2050 is expected in sub-Saharan Africa, while fertility in most of Europe, East Asia and the Americas is below the replacement rate and those populations are ageing or already shrinking. Japan, Italy, South Korea and China now face the political problems of a falling working-age population.

United Nations projections have a peak of about 10.3 billion in the 2080s, followed by decline. Debate has shifted from whether the Earth can feed its people towards consumption, emissions and the support of ageing populations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population).

name: Israel-Hamas war begins
summary: Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages; the Israeli campaign in Gaza that followed killed tens of thousands and destroyed most of the territory.
body:
Hamas and allied groups attacked southern Israel from the Gaza Strip on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and taking 251 hostages back to Gaza. It was the deadliest day for Israelis since the [founding of the state](event:israel-founded). Israel replied with an air campaign and then a ground invasion of Gaza, and the war has continued in some form since.

Gaza is a coastal strip of about 365 square kilometres holding some 2.2 million people, governed by Hamas since 2007 and under an Israeli and Egyptian blockade for most of that time. The Israeli campaign, stated as aimed at destroying Hamas and recovering the hostages, has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians according to the Gaza health ministry (a figure outside researchers regard as an undercount of total war deaths), displaced almost the entire population, often repeatedly, and destroyed or damaged most of the territory's housing, hospitals and water supply. Restrictions on aid produced famine conditions confirmed by international monitors in 2025.

The war spread beyond Gaza: exchanges with Hezbollah in Lebanon and an Israeli offensive there in 2024, attacks on shipping by the Houthis in Yemen, and direct strikes between Israel and Iran. It has produced the largest protest movements in many countries in years, deep divisions within Western governments, and proceedings at the International Court of Justice, where South Africa alleges genocide, and at the International Criminal Court, which issued arrest warrants for Israeli and Hamas leaders. Israel rejects both.

A ceasefire under an American plan began on 10 October 2025 and brought the return of the remaining hostages, living and dead, and a partial Israeli withdrawal. It has been broken repeatedly; the governance and reconstruction of Gaza are unsettled, and events are too recent for a settled account.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war).

name: Turkey-Syria earthquake
summary: A magnitude 7.8 earthquake and a 7.7 aftershock struck southern Turkey and northern Syria on 6 February 2023, killing about 60,000 people.
body:
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 struck near Gaziantep in southern Turkey at 04:17 local time on 6 February 2023, while most people were asleep. A second shock of magnitude 7.7 followed nine hours later on a neighbouring fault about 95 kilometres to the north. Together they killed around 60,000 people (some 53,500 in Turkey and between 6,000 and 8,500 in Syria) and injured more than 120,000.

The rupture ran for hundreds of kilometres along the East Anatolian Fault, where the Anatolian and Arabian plates meet. It was the strongest earthquake in Turkey since 1939 and the deadliest so far this century after the Indian Ocean tsunami and the Haiti earthquake.

Damage was made far worse by construction. Turkey has had modern seismic building codes since 1999, but they were widely ignored and repeatedly forgiven by amnesties that legalised non-compliant buildings for a fee; hundreds of thousands of homes collapsed, many of them pancaking floor onto floor. Contractors were arrested afterwards and the government was widely criticised, both for the amnesties and for the slowness of the first days of rescue.

In north-western Syria the earthquake struck a region already ruined by twelve years of civil war, holding millions of displaced people and reachable by aid only through a single border crossing, which delayed help by days. Millions were left homeless across both countries, and reconstruction has been estimated to cost well over $100 billion.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Turkey%E2%80%93Syria_earthquakes).
